Title: National debate on the reinstatement of the death penalty in Côte d’Ivoire and civil society’s position
Content: Following a rise in crime in Côte d’Ivoire, a public debate has emerged over whether the death penalty should be reinstated, having been abolished by the 2000 Constitution and reaffirmed as abolished under the 2016 Constitution. On 16 July 2026, member of Parliament Naya Jarvis Zamblé proposed opening a national debate on the reintroduction of the death penalty in Côte d’Ivoire for the most heinous crimes. In a context where the judicial system has certain weaknesses, the reintroduction of the death penalty could increase the risk of miscarriages of justice or decisions perceived as arbitrary, potentially undermining public trust in the judiciary.

Title: Closure of the Afiuni case brings 16 years of restrictions and judicial persecution to an end
Content:
On 7 August 2026, relatives of Judge María Lourdes Afiuni reported that they had received a judicial notification granting her full freedom due to the expiration of her sentence, the termination of her criminal liability, and the definitive closure of the judicial proceedings against her after 16 years.
Judge Afiuni was detained without a judicial warrant on 10 December 2009, in retaliation for granting bail to businessman Eligio Cedeño. His detention had been deemed arbitrary at the time by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention.
Following her arrest, then-President Hugo Chávez publicly called for her prosecution and a 30-year prison sentence—the maximum penalty established by the Venezuelan Constitution—while also accusing her of corruption. Judge Afiuni’s case is illustrative of the lack of judicial independence in Venezuela and the use of the judiciary as a tool of repression.
During her time in detention, there were numerous reports concerning the inhumane conditions of her imprisonment and torture. Judge Afiuni herself later revealed that she had been subjected to sexual violence. The sexual abuse she suffered resulted in a forced pregnancy, which ended in a miscarriage.
Her detention was deemed arbitrary by the United Nations Working Group on Arbitrary Detention, which called on the Venezuelan State to release her immediately in October 2010. Likewise, national and international organisations spoke out against the abuses and violations she endured throughout the proceedings.

Title: The Referendum on the New Constitution: a campaign of attacks and intimidation targeting human rights defenders who question the legality of the process, including through the use of fake profiles on digital platforms.
Content:
On 12 August 2026, on the occasion of the anniversary of the Guinean Human Rights League, its President denounced the government’s decision to call a referendum on the new Constitution as “illegal” and called for the law to be respected. His position is based, among other things, on Article 9(2) of Law No. 12/2026 of 16 June, which provides for a clear separation between the timing of a referendum and elections for the country’s national or local authorities. With general elections scheduled for 6 December, the decision to hold a referendum at this time therefore raises serious questions about its legality.
The League also argued that changes to the Constitution—particularly a document that defines how the State is organised, limits government power, and protects citizens’ rights and freedoms—should not be rushed or shaped around particular individuals, interests, or short-term political circumstances.
Later that same day, the League’s President, Abubacar Turé, was publicly attacked through a fake Facebook profile using the name “Eng. Santos Pereira” and a photograph of former President Umaro Sissoco Embaló. The post accused Turé of acting on instructions from the PAIGC and claimed that his public statement was simply the fulfilment of those instructions. It also described him as a “small fry” and a political delinquent who was unable to distinguish partisan political convictions from the independent mission of a human rights organisation, and urged people to disregard his statements as nonsense.
The incident is consistent with a broader pattern of intimidation and public attacks against human rights defenders and civil society actors who criticise alleged unlawful or abusive actions by the authorities. Those who publicly raise such concerns are frequently subjected to personal attacks, defamation and attempts to discredit their work, rather than having their concerns addressed through legal or institutional channels.

Title: Forced Dissolution of Lingnan University Students’ Union and the Eradication of Campus Civic Space
Content:
On 7 August 2026, the Lingnan University Students’ Union (LingU SU) announced its official disbandment, ending 59 years of independent student representation. In its dissolution statement, the union cited profound "changes in the environment inside and outside the campus." A former vice-president of the union revealed that the organisation had been functionally paralysed over the past year and was completely unable to organise student activities. Furthermore, university management had stonewalled the union, demonstrating an active unwillingness to communicate or acknowledge their representative status.
Crucially, this dissolution follows severe legal harassment against LingU SU leadership. In June 2025, four current and former LingU SU members—including the Vice-President, who simultaneously served as the chair of the Hong Kong Federation of Students (HKFS)—were arrested for alleged "theft" and "conspiracy to steal" union funds. HKFS disbanded in February 2026.

Title: Arrest and release two days later of two civil society actors in Kimpese
Content:
On 12 August 2026, two civil society actors were arrested: Mr. Raymond Tona Tona, President of the Civil Society Consultation Framework – Forces Vives of Songololo Territory, and Mr. Luzayadio Nsungani, President of the Association of Persons Living with Disabilities/Kimpese. They were arrested at the instigation of officials from the National Electricity Company (SNEL) in Kimpese and were transferred on 13 August 2026 to the Mbanza-Ngungu High Court.
SNEL had filed a complaint against the two civil society actors, unjustly accusing them of incitement to disobedience and incitement to rebellion for carrying out their role in protecting the rights of the population of Kimpese. In particular, they had called for transparent and fair electricity tariffs before electricity bills were redistributed in Kimpese. Source
On 14 August 2026, the two detained civil society actors were released.

Title: Arrest of two civil society actors, in Kimpese, Kongo Central Province
Content:
Two civil society actors, Mr. TONA TONA Raymond, President of the Civil Society Consultation Framework/Forces Vives of Songololo Territory, and Mr. LUZAYADIO NSUNGANI, President of the Association of Persons Living with Disabilities in Kimpese, were arrested on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, at around 2:00 p.m. in Kimpese, Kongo Central Province.
According to information received by VSV, several civil society organisations in Kimpese held a meeting on Saturday, 8 August 2026, to discuss the issue of flat-rate billing by the National Electricity Company (SNEL) for the population’s electricity consumption. During the meeting, the civil society actors decided, among other things, that the population should not accept the electricity bills for July 2026 and should return them to the sender.
The two civil society actors were subsequently summoned to the office of the Congolese National Police (PNC) in Kimpese, where they were questioned. Mr. TONA TONA was questioned on Wednesday, 12 August 2026, while Mr. LUZAYADIO was questioned the previous day, Tuesday, 11 August 2026. They were then arrested at the time indicated above at the PNC Territorial District Headquarters in Kimpese.
Following their arrest, they were taken to the PNC camp, where they remain detained as of the time of writing.

Title: Verdict scheduled for landmark subversion case against disbanded Hong Kong Alliance leaders
Content:
The High Court has formally scheduled its verdict for 21 August 2026 at 10:00 am in the landmark National Security Law (NSL) case HKSAR v. Hong Kong Alliance in Support of Patriotic Democratic Movements of China, Lee Cheuk-yan, and Chow Hang-tung (Case No: HCCC 155/2022). The disbanded organisation and its former leaders are charged with "incitement to subversion of state power" under Articles 22 and 23 of the NSL. The verdict will be handed down by a panel of designated National Security judges: Justices Alex Lee Wan-tang, Johnny Chan Chung-heng, and Anna Lai Yuen-kee.
By the date of the verdict, Lee Cheuk-yan and Chow Hang-tung will have been remanded in custody for nearly 1,800 days (almost five years) since their initial charges and detention in September 2021. The prosecution centres on the Alliance's decades-long peaceful advocacy, including the organisation of the annual Victoria Park candlelight vigils commemorating the 1989 Tiananmen Square crackdown and its core political platform calling for the end of one-party rule in China. If convicted, the defendants face maximum penalties of up to life imprisonment.

Title: State threats and aggressive intimidation against the Hong Kong Journalists Association ahead of elections
Content:
On 7 August 2026, the day before the Hong Kong Journalists Association (HKJA) Executive Committee election, Secretary for Security Chris Tang launched a severe verbal attack against the union. Tang accused unnamed groups of "abusing the name of trade unions" and issued a direct warning: "If you endanger national security, we will definitely nail you down" (如危害國安一定會釘死你). He further criticised the HKJA for declining to make its candidate list public prior to the vote, calling it a "black-box" operation.
In response, HKJA chairperson Selina Cheng clarified that the decision to conceal the candidate list from the public before the meeting was made strictly to protect candidates from intense intimidation and harassment campaigns. She confirmed that the full executive list is legally submitted to the Registry of Trade Unions annually following the election. Despite the threats, the HKJA held its election on the morning of 8 August 2026 in a closed-door meeting attended by approximately 30 members. Five executive committee members were elected. During the meeting, suspected plainclothes police were observed monitoring the venue from vehicles outside. When questioned by the press about whether law enforcement possessed concrete evidence of national security crimes against the HKJA, Tang stated that his warning was targeted at "everyone," reiterating that police would "use all methods to find evidence" and pursue arrests and prosecutions.

Title: Internal leadership dispute within HRDC raises concerns over coalition governance, legitimacy and the integrity of human rights advocacy in Malawi
Content:
The Human Rights Defenders Coalition (HRDC), one of Malawi's prominent platforms for human rights and democratic governance advocacy, is experiencing a prolonged internal leadership and governance dispute involving competing claims over the legitimacy of its current leadership, the need to convene an Annual General Meeting (AGM), financial accountability, and the authority to speak on behalf of the coalition.
Concerns became public in February 2026, when members from different regions challenged the failure to hold an AGM since 2019 and questioned the legitimacy of the provisional leadership headed by Mr. Michael Kaiyatsa. The concerned members called for an AGM to elect leadership and also raised concerns regarding access to organisational and financial information.
The dispute subsequently escalated into legal proceedings. On 27 April 2026 an HRDC ad hoc committee had taken the HRDC leadership to court, seeking judicial intervention and calling for an AGM and disclosure of donor funding.
The dispute remains unresolved. On 23 July 2026, the High Court proceedings resulted in competing interpretations of the outcome, with the parties subsequently disagreeing publicly over whether the court had effectively rejected the challenge to the current leadership or had instead identified governance gaps requiring mediation.
The continuing conflict risks weakening HRDC's institutional credibility, internal cohesion and capacity to provide coordinated human rights advocacy.

Respect and protection: Freedom of association

Title: Government-led forced evictions in Wabari, Mogadishu trigger civilian protest and alleged use of live ammunition
Content:
On 13 August 2026, residents of Wabari district in Mogadishu protested against forced evictions and the demolition of homes and businesses. Residents said families were being removed from their homes without adequate alternatives and called for an end to the demolitions. Local reporting indicated that government security forces used live ammunition against residents resisting the evictions, with protesters reporting that at least one civilian was wounded and taken to hospital.
The incident has intensified concerns over government-led land demolitions and forced displacement in Mogadishu. Residents and opposition figures have accused authorities of unlawful evictions and land grabbing, while the wider issue has generated repeated protests and political tensions in the capital.
The event is significant for the enabling environment because it concerns the rights of affected communities to housing, security and peaceful civic participation, as well as the state's response to citizens protesting decisions that directly affect their homes and livelihoods.

Title: Appeals court overturns Sadia Moalim Ali’s conviction and orders her release after 123 days in detention
Content:
On 12 August 2026, the Banaadir Regional Court of Appeal overturned the three-year prison sentence imposed on Somali social activist Sadia Moalim Ali and ordered her release after 123 days in detention. Sadia had been arrested in Mogadishu on 12 April 2026 in connection with her activism, including her social media activity and participation in peaceful protests. She was subsequently convicted and sentenced to three years in prison on 25 June 2026. Amnesty International had described her detention and conviction as arbitrary and campaigned for her immediate and unconditional release.
The appeals court decision represents a significant judicial development concerning freedom of expression and peaceful civic participation in Somalia. The Coalition of Somali Human Rights Defenders welcomed her release and called for continued protection, justice and accountability. The case had generated sustained attention from Somali and international human rights actors and civil society organizations.
The decision has a positive impact on the enabling environment because it provides judicial redress in a case involving fundamental freedoms and demonstrates that an appeal process can provide a mechanism for challenging a restrictive lower-court decision.

Title: Civil Society Calls for Human Rights and the Release of People Detained for Political Reasons to Be Central to the New Dialogue Process
Content:
On 1 August 2026, a formal process of political dialogue and negotiation was launched between authorities of Delcy Rodríguez’s interim government and representatives of the National Assembly elected in 2015.
Although this represents another attempt at political negotiation, the process has three distinctive characteristics. First, it is taking place seven months after the U.S. military intervention in Venezuelan territory. Second, the United States government is the initiative’s main sponsor and will act as an observer of the process. Third, the dialogue is taking place between the core leadership of the 2015 National Assembly and officials of the interim government, led by the current President of the National Assembly.
In this regard, the priority objective of the process will be to strengthen democratic institutions, including the electoral system and the restoration of other political rights. The initial agreed agenda is based on three areas: addressing the needs of earthquake victims, strengthening democracy, and political rights and guarantees.
However, the actual agenda is broader, including progress on civil and political rights, a process of re-institutionalising the Supreme Court of Justice and the National Electoral Council. According to information reported by the media and other sources, the aim is to achieve progress in these three areas between October and December of this year.
Several Venezuelan civil society organisations have agreed that, regardless of the initiatives adopted, the country’s democratic recovery and re-institutionalisation require the full recognition of all citizens’ rights, the unconditional release of all people detained for political reasons, and the establishment of guarantees of non-repetition.

Title: Resignation of Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources
Content:
On 11 August 2026, the Prime Minister's Office issued a Press Release announcing the voluntary resignation of two Cabinet Ministers, that of the Ministry of Home Affairs and the Ministry of Energy and Natural Resources.
In his position as the Minister for Home Affairs, Lyonpo Tshering was serving as the Chairperson of the Civil Society Organisation Authority (CSOA). His resignation comes on moral grounds, amidst an ongoing personal matter that was circulating online, and was seen as affecting public trust and integrity and the need to uphold high standards of governance. During his tenure as the Home Minister and the CSO Authority Chairperson, he supported the work by the sector and had been visiting and meeting with officials of the CSOs to understand and learn more about the sector as well as identify how the Government could work with the CSOs. In 2024, 16 CSOs, largely those working in the social sector also received a total of Nu.300 million from the Government.
The National Assembly Speaker, Lungten Dorji will replace the outgoing Minister as the next Home Minister, and Mr. Tshering will continue to serve as a Member of Parliament.

Title: Reported arrests of artists  in Western Province raises concerns over freedom of expression, political participation and fundamental rights
Content:
On 5 August 2026, Zambian police reportedly arrested musicians, a comedian and political supporters in the Mongu/Kalabo area in Western Province, in connection with alleged conduct likely to cause a breach of the peace. Those reportedly arrested included musician Moses Ng’andwe, popularly known as Chester; Felix Ndangeni Inshila; and comedian Winston Ngosa, popularly known as IDC Light Comedy.
The reported arrests occurred in the lead-up to Zambia’s 13 August 2026 General Election and involved public personalities reportedly associated with political activities and mobilization for the opposition party, the National Reconciliation Party for Unity and Prosperity (NRPUP), in the area. The circumstances have raised concerns regarding the exercise of freedom of expression and political participation during a sensitive electoral period.
The Comedy Association of Zambia and the Zambia Music Association have confirmed the arrests of their respective members and have called for their release. The associations' confirmation further corroborates the reported arrests and highlights concerns within the creative sector about how artists are treated during the electoral period.

Title: India’s Gen Z rises — Youth protests and activist Sonam Wangchuk’s 26-Day Hunger Strike force the Union Education Minister’s Resignation over Exam-Integrity failures.
Content:
In July 2026, a youth-led movement over examination integrity grew into one of India’s most significant civic mobilisations in recent memory — and, unusually, one that forced a concrete result. Triggered by the leak of the National Eligibility cum Entrance Test (Undergraduate) NEET-UG 2026 medical entrance paper, students and young people took to the streets and to social media in large numbers, converging on Delhi’s Jantar Mantar to demand fair examinations, government accountability, and the resignation of the Union Education Minister. The mobilisation, associated with the self-described Cockroach Janta Party (CJP), drew significant participation from students and young people and developed through both online mobilisation and street demonstrations.
Key developments:

28 June 2026 — Renowned Ladakhi environmental activist Sonam Wangchuk began an indefinite hunger strike at Jantar Mantar in solidarity with the students, demanding examination reforms and accountability.
In July 2026, Gen Z and student protesters mobilised across India, particularly in Delhi, over alleged examination irregularities and demanded government accountability, including the resignation of Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan.
24 July 2026 — Wangchuk ended his fast on its 26th day, following government assurances, including a commitment by the Prime Minister to take “strict action” on examination mismanagement.
25 July 2026 — Union Education Minister Dharmendra Pradhan resigned — a central demand of the movement. The government ordered a Central Bureau of Investigation probe, cancelled the compromised exam, conducted a re-test, and announced NEET’s shift to a computer-based format from 2027.
July–August 2026 — In Jharkhand, students and government job aspirants continued protests over alleged irregularities in the Jharkhand Public Service Commission and Jharkhand Staff Selection Commission recruitment examinations, demanding transparency and investigation.

These developments reflect growing youth participation in civic affairs through protests, hunger strikes and digital mobilisation, while also highlighting concerns regarding examination governance, government accountability, and the protection of peaceful assembly and expression. Specifically, the reported restrictions on demonstrations, the denial of protest permits beyond Jantar Mantar, and alleged use of force against protesters raise real concerns about the proportionality of the state’s response and the space available for dissent. The movement is therefore both a powerful example of civic participation and a reminder of how precarious the right to protest, especially for young people, can be.
Enabling principles: 1. Respect and protection of fundamental freedoms | 5. Supportive public culture and discourses on civil society
Respect and protection: Freedom of assembly

Title: Promises of Transparency Without Updated Information on the Destination of Oil Revenues
Content:
In January 2026, shortly after Delcy Rodríguez assumed office as Acting President of the Republic, the government announced the creation of two funds through which resources generated by the country’s oil activity would be channelled: the Social Protection Fund and the Infrastructure and Services Fund.
In this regard, the Acting President announced the creation of a digital platform that would be used to make information on the management of these funds and resources publicly available. Thus, in March, the official “Sovereign Transparency” portal was created and presented as a mechanism for monitoring and accountability.
At the time of its launch, the platform reported an income of USD 300 million from an oil-sector transaction which, according to the information displayed on the platform, had been allocated to the Social Protection Fund.
However, despite the promises of greater monitoring and transparency in the management of public revenues from the oil sector, the portal has not been updated since 13 March and continues to display the same figure cited above, with no changes.
This issue has been highlighted by Transparencia Venezuela, and is particularly significant given the scale of revenues generated in 2026, which, according to its estimates, have ranged between USD 6 billion and USD 8 billion. To date, however, the destination of these resources has not been disclosed, despite the government’s own announcements at the beginning of the year.
This situation represents a continuation of the policy of opacity that has characterised access to public information in the country, particularly regarding the management of public resources, as updated information remains unavailable.

Title: ECZ Nationwide suspension of results announcement raises concerns over peaceful and credible elections in Zambia
Content:
On 14 August 2026, the Electoral Commission of Zambia (ECZ) temporarily suspended vote counting and the announcement of results following reports of violence against election officials and theft of ballot papers during the 13 August general elections. The suspension affected the presidential and parliamentary results.
According to Reuters, the ECZ lifted the suspension later on 14 August after determining that the security threat had been contained. ECZ Chairperson Mwangala Zaloumis stated that results would be announced progressively and warned candidates against declaring themselves winners before the official results. Final presidential results were expected by 17 August.
The interruption occurred amid heightened political tensions. Opposition candidate Brian Mundubile claimed his party had won, while President Hakainde Hichilema urged citizens to remain patient and peaceful. The ECZ reiterated that only the Commission has authority to announce official results.

Title: Escalation of restrictions on the cooperative sector: weakened promotion policies, suspensions and withdrawal of operating authorisations
Content:
On 31 July 2026, INAES Resolution No. 1556/2026 was published, through which the Argentine State moved from suspending to withdrawing the operating authorisation of a group of cooperatives that had remained suspended since the oversight process initiated in 2024. Under the Cooperatives Law, the withdrawal of operating authorisation constitutes grounds for the dissolution of the entity.
The measure represents a further step within a broader process that has altered the institutional conditions for establishing, sustaining and developing cooperatives, forms of collective economic organisation in which members engage in productive and service activities under a democratic governance structure. Since 2024, this process has been marked by the suspension of 7,873 cooperatives and 417 mutual associations, the requirement of a minimum of six members to establish certain cooperatives, which hinders small-scale collective organisation, a reduction in promotion and financing programmes and instruments, and increased administrative requirements.
These measures particularly affect organisations with more limited administrative and financial capacity, which are simultaneously facing a reduction in State support mechanisms and stronger oversight and sanctioning mechanisms. While the State has the authority to supervise compliance with legal obligations, the reduction in State support and the strengthening of oversight may make it more difficult for organisations to regularise their status and remain sustainable.
In this context, the withdrawal of operating authorisations contributes to a deterioration of the enabling environment for the cooperative sector and poses a risk of further contraction of a sector that provides a space for economic organisation and collective participation.

Title: Organizers of 2023 protests granted house arrest while criminalization proceedings continue
Content:
On 4 August 2026, the Third Criminal Court granted house arrest to Luis Pacheco and Héctor Chaclán, former authorities of the 48 Cantons of Totonicapán, who had spent one year and three months in preventive detention. Both were arrested on 23 April 2025 and are being prosecuted for terrorism and obstruction of criminal action in relation to their role in the mobilizations following the 2023 general elections. The protests arose in response to the actions by the Public Prosecutor's Office against the electoral process and became a broad expression of citizen participation and defense of the election results and the democratic order, led by indigenous authorities and different social sectors. During the period of Pacheco’s and Chaclán’s detention, hearings to review the coercive measures were suspended or rescheduled on several occasions.
The resolution replaces preventive detention with house arrest and establishes a financial bond of Q160 thousand for each as well as the obligation to appear monthly before the Public Prosecutor's Office, the prohibition of leaving the country without judicial authorization, and the impossibility of holding public office while the process continues. The measure represents progress with respect to their right to freedom, however, the criminal process remains open.
During the same hearing, the court complied with a resolution of the Fourth Chamber of Appeals that ordered them to also be prosecuted for illicit association, a crime that adds to the accusations of terrorism and obstruction of criminal action. Likewise, the intermediate stage hearing was rescheduled for September 22, 2026.
The case continues to be relevant to the enabling environment of civil society organizations due to its implications for the right to protest, citizen participation, and the exercise of the collective rights of indigenous authorities and leaders. Although the substitution of pretrial detention is a step forward, the continuity and expansion of the criminal process maintain concerns about possible inhibiting effects on social mobilization and participation.
Civil society needs to maintain the monitoring of the judicial proceedings, respect for the guarantees of due process and the conditions imposed on both former leaders. The evolution of the case will make it possible to assess whether there are additional advances in the protection of their rights or if conditions persist that could generate restrictive effects on indigenous authorities, community leaders and other civil society actors linked to protest and citizen participation.

Title: Mohamed Bakir Turki remanded in custody on charges relating to terrorism and his online comments
Content:
On 12 August 2026, the investigating judge at the Sidi M’Hamed Court in Algiers ordered the remand in custody of Mohamed Bakir Turki, known as ‘Sofiane’, at Koléa Prison. The activist had been arrested at his place of work on 9 August 2026 and held in police custody prior to his appearance in court. He is being prosecuted, amongst other things, for “glorifying terrorism” and for using information and communication technologies to support or disseminate the ideas of a terrorist organisation, as well as for spreading false information likely to undermine public order, harm the national interest, show contempt for the authorities and incite a boycott of the elections. The charges are reportedly based, in particular, on his participation in a TikTok live stream broadcast on 5 June 2026.
Mohamed Bakir Turki is particularly well known for having coined the phrase ‘Yetnahaw Gaâ’ in 2019, which has become one of the iconic slogans of the Hirak. This case raises concerns about the use of anti-terrorism provisions and public order offences against political statements posted on social media, with a potential chilling effect on freedom of expression and civic participation in Algeria.

Title: Suppression of criticism of government continues with arrest of two netizens
Content:
Based on a complaint filed on 4 August 2026, the Cyber Crime Directorate of the West Java Regional Police has arrested two men, AYP (49) and AF (40), over posts they had made on the social media platform Threads. They are charged with incitement or provocation under the Electronic Information and Transactions (ITE) Law for allegedly editing and sharing a provocative post about Prabowo’s speech, in which she aid that Iran has nuclear weapons. At the time of reporting, the Presidential Palace had not issued a substantive response and referred inquiries to the police.
Civil society groups like Amnesty International Indonesia and YLBHI are monitoring the case, with Amnesty International Indonesia condemning the arrests as repressive. The incident is part of a broader pattern of the ITE law being used in broad ways to criminalise online posts commenting on official statements or otherwise being critical of the government. The arrested men now face a maximum prison sentence of 2 years and a maximum fine of 200 million IDR (ca. 10,000 Euro).

Title: Sham parliament approves Anti-Online Scam Bill introducing capital punishment amid ongoing military complicity
Content:
On 28 July 2026, the sham Pyidaungsu Hluttaw (the joint Lower and Upper Houses) in Naypyidaw passed the sweeping "Anti-Online Scam Bill," officially enacted as Pyidaungsu Hluttaw Law No. 3/2026 on 31 July 2026. The legislation establishes severe legal penalties aimed at dismantling transnational cyber-fraud syndicates that have flourished in Myanmar's border regions. Crucially, the bill authorizes capital punishment for operators, guards, or managers who utilize violence, torture, illegal abductions, or forced detention to coerce individuals into cyber fraud operations, particularly if such abuse results in a victim's death. Furthermore, it mandates maximum sentences of life in prison for individuals directly operating online scam centers or committing cryptocurrency fraud.
The passage of this bill marks the first major piece of criminal legislation enacted by the new pseudo-civilian administration led by the Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) following the regime's heavily orchestrated 2025-26 sham elections. The legislative push comes as the junta faces mounting diplomatic pressure from China and the United States to crack down on industrial-scale scam compounds. During 22-24 July 2026, the junta and junta-aligned Democratic Karen Benevolent Army (DKBA) have moved thousands of foreign nationals working in their scam site from Kyaukkhet area first to Sonseemyaing village, the headquarters of DKBA, and then to the Payathonzu (Three Pagodas Pass) area in Karen State. 
However, the Karen National Union (KNU) and resistance groups remain deeply skeptical, noting that recent crackdowns and deportations have largely resulted in scam outfits merely relocating to other border regions rather than ceasing operations, largely due to the deep complicity of pro-junta Border Guard Forces (BGF) and military-aligned militias that directly profit from leasing land to these criminal enterprises.

Title: Election process for Ombudsman office begins with concerns about repeated political influence
Content:
On 10 August 2026, the deadline for registration of candidates for Ombudsman and Deputy Ombudsman closed. The call for registrations had previously been made by the Senate in accordance with the requirements established in the National Constitution and in Organic Law No. 631/95. With the registration process closed and given the significance of the role, renewed concerns about potential political influence and the impact of the Ombudsman’s office have been raised.
The important figure of the Ombudsman was introduced with the Magna Carta of 1992, but his previous performance did not live up to expectations regarding its impact on the defense of human rights, the protection of community interests, and the receiving and management of popular complaints. Specialists in the area indicate that the institutions has shown deficits, particularly in terms of being influenced by party-political agendas, undermining its intended role. As a result, in 2014, the institution had been disqualified by the Subcommittee on Accreditation of the Global Alliance of National Human Rights Institutions, citing a lack of transparency in the election process and lack of independence in the fulfilment of its mandate. Since then, the integrity of the institution improved receiving a “B” grade in 2019 and an “A” rating in 2025. Previous concerns nevertheless highlight the need for appointing a suitable person able to contribute to the democratic construction of public policies to the prioritization of indigenous peoples' communities, peasant communities and LGBTIQ+ groups, among others. While it is expected that the new appointments will be independent, press reports have already warned about the candidacy of the current deputy Ombudsman, who remains registered in the registry of the governing party (ANR), despite the fact that the regulations require the suspension of party affiliation while in office. The upcoming appointment is therefore under scrutiny for its potential impact on citizen’s confidence in democratic institutions, government transparency and accountability to civil society, and the significance of the Ombudsman’s office for strengthening rule of law and empowering civil society monitoring.
Following the registration of candidates, it is the responsibility of the Senate to form shortlists on all the nominations made, which will then be referred to the Chamber of Deputies, where the election will proceed, by a two-thirds majority, of those who will exercise the Ombudsman's Office, as head and as alternate for the period 2026-2031.

Title: Unlawful eviction and criminalisation of the Mbyá Guaraní community signals deteriorating environment for indigenous rights activism
Content:
On 28 July 2026, some 50 members of the Misiones Police forcibly evicted seven families from the Mbyá Guaraní Puente Quemado II Community (Garuhapé), transferring them in a cage truck, at the request of forestry businessman Alfredo Ruff. The evictions were originally ordered by the regional court in the area but had been appealed and happened on ancestral lands recognized by the National Institute of Indigenous Affairs (INAI, Resolution 514/2015). The Prosecutor's Office of Instruction I of Puerto Rico questioned the irregularity of the measure due to extreme institutional gravity, and the families recovered their territory on August 2.
The situation further escalated subsequently with Ruff proposing via his Instagram account that he would resolve the conflict himself insinuating shooting at people in the community and the militant of La Libertad Avanza, the ruling party at the national level, Roberto Bonetti responding that he was in favor of solving it "by shooting" if necessary. Days later, Ruff's lawyer – former judge Osvaldo Lunge – requested the arrest of two members of the Missionary Team of the Aboriginal Pastoral (EMIPA) who accompany the community, the seizure of the vehicles that transport people to the territory, and the intervention of the Gendarmerie, alleging that that armed foreigners were in the area and children and women were being extorted. EMiPA, REGCHAG and Rebellion or Extinction Misiones denounced the incitement to violence and blamed the Judiciary and different departments of the provincial government for inaction; the community and EMiPA decided to go to UN human rights mechanisms due to the lack of provincial guarantees. At the same time, activists from "Rebellion or Extinction Missions" are organizing a collection of food, money and tools in Posadas to rebuild the homes destroyed during the eviction.
The evictions, filing of charges and threats against community members and civil society organisations supporting them illustrate how the environment for the defense of indigenous peoples’ rights is deteriorating. The fact that the evictions were carried out despite recognition of the ancestral land and an ongoing appeal adds to legal insecurity for indigenous communities and organisations, who denounce that their existing constitutional rights were ignored and ancestral permanence was labelled as ‘usurpation’. Further, the threats of violence generate a chilling effect that seeks to paralyze organized communities and the activists that accompany them.
The evictions also happened in a broader context of dismantling indigenous peoples’ rights protection and advancing extractivist and private economic interests. Policies and institutions for the protection of indigenous peoples’ rights have continuously been weakened with attempts to defund the INAI and the repeal of Law 26.160 which had previously suspended evictions from indigenous lands. Taken together with the criminalization of indigenous leaders and those accompanying them, the event shows an increasingly disabling environment for civil society working in the field of indigenous peoples’ rights.

Title: Composition of the Postulation Commission opens key stage for the election of the Comptroller General of Accounts
Content:
On 7 August 2026, with the election of the representatives of the College of Public Accountants and Auditors of Guatemala, the Nomination Commission responsible for preparing a shortlist of six candidates for the position of Comptroller General of Accounts for the 2026–2030 term was established. The shortlist will subsequently be submitted to Congress, which must elect the new head of the Office of the Comptroller General of Accounts (CGC) with the favourable vote of at least 81 deputies.
The Commission will be chaired by Miquel Cortés, Rector of Universidad Rafael Landívar, elected by the Forum of University Rectors, and will comprise the deans of the relevant faculties of universities across the country and representatives of professional associations established under the applicable regulations. Its role is to assess and select candidates based on criteria of merit, capacity, suitability and integrity.
Following its establishment, the commissioners will need to be sworn in and determine the venue for the sessions, the work schedule and the mechanisms for receiving and assessing applicants’ files. The Commission must submit the shortlist of six candidates to Congress by 23 September at the latest, while the election of the new Comptroller must take place before 13 October 2026.
The upcoming stage will be relevant for civil society organisations, as the establishment of the Commission opens an important space for observation, monitoring and advocacy. Access to the sessions, applicants’ files, assessment criteria, scoring tables and decisions taken will allow for monitoring compliance with the principles of publicity, transparency and independence throughout the selection process for the person who will lead a key institution responsible for overseeing public resources.

Title: Constitutional Court reinforces access to information on government use of surveillance technologies
Content:
On 4 August 2026, it was reported that the Constitutional Chamber upheld a writ of amparo (a constitutional protection action) against the Ministry of Finance for failing to fulfill its duty to provide a clear, complete, and legally sufficient response to a citizen's request regarding the potential use of technologies developed by the Israeli Mossad to combat tax evasion and smuggling. The request sought information on, among other things, the legal framework for these tools, their possible use for mass data processing and profiling, safeguards against cyber espionage, auditing mechanisms, and the protection of personal data.
The Ministry of Finance initially failed to respond within the allotted timeframe and, after being notified of the appeal for constitutional protection, provided a response that the Constitutional Chamber deemed generic, as it did not address the inquiries individually nor justify why certain questions could not be answered. The Court considered that the rights established in Articles 27 and 30 of the Political Constitution had been violated and ordered a comprehensive response within ten business days.
While the Ministry of Finance is the institution directly involved, the implications also extend to other entities responsible for data protection, digital governance, cybersecurity and institutional control, as well as civil society organizations working on transparency, privacy, digital rights and accountability.

Title: Junta and UEC escalate legal restrictions on political parties, candidate qualifications, and foreign diplomatic contacts
Content:
Throughout July 2026, the junta-controlled Union Election Commission (UEC) and the military regime enacted a series of draconian regulatory and legislative amendments to further restrict political parties and parliamentary candidate qualifications. On 2 July 2026, the UEC amended Section 25(f) of its By-laws, seizing sole authority to decide whether lawmakers from dissolved parties can retain their seats or run again. Simultaneously, amendments to Section 24 mandated that party patrons and Central Executive Committee (CEC) members meet the same strict qualifications as parliamentary candidates, while requiring parties to submit CEC lists within 30 days of registration and report any changes within seven days.
On 14 July 2026, the junta introduced a bill amending Section 8(c) of the Election Laws, raising candidate educational requirements from a basic high school level to a mandatory recognized university degree from Burma—a requirement that now automatically applies to CEC members and patrons as well. On 27 July 2026, the UEC intensified party surveillance by ordering political parties to re-verify membership lists, demonstrate physical offices, and formally report all interactions with foreign embassies and diplomats. This follows stricter organizational thresholds requiring nationwide parties to maintain 50,000 members and 110 township offices, leaving only six of the 57 registered parties able to operate nationally. Prominent party chairs, including from the Rakhine Nationalities Party (RNP) and Democratic Party, highlighted that these rules create insurmountable barriers due to conflict dynamics and restrict legitimate diplomatic engagement.

Title: Junta troops abduct and execute LGBTQ+ youth humanitarian aid workers during clearance operation for Russian-backed Dawei SEZ
Content:
On 9 July 2026, junta troops in Yebyu Township, Tanintharyi Region, abducted three LGBTQ+ youth humanitarian aid workers and an unidentified male civilian from Kamauk Chaung village to use as human shields. The victims were members of the local civil relief team The Ants (Humanitarian Aids Team-Tanintharyi) and were in the area providing emergency humanitarian assistance to local villagers. The abducted humanitarian workers were identified as Ko Athar (24), team leader and student at Dawei University of Education; Ko Myat Thu (19), team member; and Ko Leon (24), finance officer and student at the National University of Computer Studies.
On 13 July 2026, local residents discovered the disfigured, severely decomposed bodies of the four victims between Wazundaw and Akani villages. A director from the local human rights group MAGGA Initiative reported that the stage of decomposition indicated the victims were executed four or five days prior. Residents confirmed their identities through ID cards found in a nearby bag. Local sources suspect the junta troops executed the workers after searching their seized mobile phones and laptops and discovering documentation of their humanitarian relief work. This violent operation followed a 22 June 2026 directive by deputy junta military chief Kyaw Swar Lin, who ordered troops to "wipe out" resistance along National Highway No. 8 to secure the Russian-backed Dawei Special Economic Zone (SEZ) mega-project.

Title: Union concerns over government transparency and engagement over Hilton Trinidad workers’ job security
Content: On 4 August 2026, Hilton International Trinidad Ltd informed the Communication Workers’ Union (CWU) that its lease for the Hilton Trinidad and Conference Centre expires on September 18, 2026, and that it may be unable to continue operating the hotel beyond that date if a replacement agreement with State-owned eTeCK is not finalised. More than 250 workers are affected by the uncertainty. Employees have also been provided with estimates of potential severance benefits should their employment end. The development follows public assurances made in June by Land and Legal Affairs Minister Saddam Hosein that workers would not be affected and that their jobs were safe. The CWU has therefore questioned the apparent discrepancy between these assurances and the subsequent severance calculations and uncertainty surrounding employment after 18 September 2026. The union has requested clarity on workers’ continued employment, accumulated service and benefits, and whether they would be retained if another operator assumes responsibility for the hotel. The CWU has also written to Minister Hosein requesting a meeting but, as of 10 August, had received no response. Guardian Media similarly reported receiving no response from the Minister by press time. This situation has a direct knock-on effect on the enabling environment for civil society organisations, as it places the CWU in a position where it must urgently seek information and engage State actors in order to fulfil its representative function, while facing limited responsiveness from the authorities.

Title: Government introduces Draft NGO Registration and Supervision Bill
Content:
In late July 2026, the Government of Sri Lanka initiated the process of introducing the Non-Governmental Organization Registration and Supervision Bill by sharing the amended draft with the National Collective of Civil Society Organizations (CSOs) and NGOs through the National Secretariat for Non-Governmental Organizations (NGO Secretariat). A stakeholder consultation, chaired by Mr. Sampath Manthreenayake, Secretary to the Ministry of Rural Development, Social Protection and Community Empowerment, was held on 20 July 2026, following which the NGO Secretariat invited the NGO Collective to submit written observations and recommendations on the draft Bill. Nevertheless, the limited engagement with CSOs prior to drafting is problematic given the Bill's wide application to grassroots organizations, including trade unions, alumni associations, and informal community groups. 
The proposed Bill is justified by the government as a measure to strengthen compliance with the Financial Action Task Force (FATF) standards and reduce the risks of money laundering, terrorist financing, and proliferation financing. While these objectives are acknowledged, the current draft has raised significant concerns regarding overregulation, excessive executive discretion, and its potential impact on civic space.
 The Bill establishes a new Competent Authority despite the existing NGO Secretariat, adopts an overly broad scope that extends to informal community groups, and lacks clarity regarding the Authority's independence, governance, and accountability. It also grants extensive inspection powers, subjects the Authority to ministerial directions, makes registration a prerequisite for operation, requires renewal every three years, and provides no clear grounds for refusal, timelines, reasons for decisions, or appeal mechanisms. Additional concerns relate to restrictions on advocacy during pre-election periods and broad powers to suspend organizations for activities deemed inconsistent with their stated objectives. 
Therefore, proceeding with the Bill in its current form risks significantly deteriorating the enabling environment for civil society in Sri Lanka by imposing extensive administrative requirements and granting broad, insufficiently constrained powers to the executive. Without clear safeguards, transparent decision-making and effective avenues for appeal, these provisions risk being used to restrict legitimate civic activity. The Government should therefore substantially revise the Bill through meaningful and inclusive consultation with CSOs to ensure that efforts to strengthen regulatory oversight do not come at the expense of civic freedoms, organizational autonomy and democratic participation.

Title: Reactivation of the Human Rights Network of Panama
Content: On 16 July 2026, around 15 Panamanian civil society organisations and activists met to  (i) formally reactivate the Panamanian Human Rights Network, (ii) merge with the Citizens’ Alliance for Justice, and (iii) elect a new Board of Directors for the 2026–2028 term.The main objective is to resume a unified agenda for the defence of human rights defenders—covering civil and political rights as well as social, cultural and environmental rights - and the protection of civic space, moving away from ad hoc responses towards permanent coordination. It was agreed to implement an early warning system and a national register of cases of harassment or criminalisation of human rights defenders. This alliance aims to ensure that harassment directed at specific sectors - such as indigenous communities, trade unions or environmentalists - is recognised as a collective threat to civil society as a whole.

Title: Prime Minister publicly criticises Emancipation Support Committee following 2026 Emancipation Day celebrations
Content:
On 1 August 2026, during African Emancipation Day activities organised by the Emancipation Support Committee of Trinidad and Tobago (ESCTT), Culture Minister Michelle Benjamin was challenged by members of the public and later booed during parts of the celebrations. ESCTT representatives reportedly intervened and reminded attendees that the event was non-partisan and that guests should be treated respectfully. Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar, who had been listed as a featured speaker at the Emancipation Village, did not attend. She later said that she had never committed to attend the event and responded strongly to criticism surrounding her absence.
In the days that followed, the Prime Minister criticised the ESCTT over its handling of the treatment of Minister Benjamin and reportedly alleged political interference. She also mentioned that she had lost respect for the organisation and that her relationship with the organisation has been “irreparably damaged”. The ESCTT publicly rejected this account. It said Benjamin had not been placed in danger, that committee members had intervened when necessary, and that the organisation remained non-partisan. ESCTT representatives said they did not want the disagreement to develop into a political “back and forth” and expressed concern that the discussion around Emancipation had become increasingly divisive.
Public criticism by the Head of Government of a prominent CSO in connection with alleged “political interference” can contribute to a more cautious operating climate, particularly for organisations involved in cultural, advocacy or rights-related work. Even in the absence of formal sanctions, such rhetoric may increase perceived risks for CSOs when engaging in public debate or hosting events where political figures are present. Over time, this can have a negative effect on civic space by discouraging organisations from taking visible or critical positions, or by prompting them to self-censor in order to avoid political backlash.

Title: Government initiates legal reform process to strengthen recognition and protection of intersex persons in Zimbabwe
Content:
On 5 August 2026, during a high-level breakfast meeting held in Harare, the Government of Zimbabwe indicated that it had begun taking steps towards addressing gaps in the country’s legal and policy framework affecting intersex persons. The meeting, officially opened by the Minister of Justice, Legal and Parliamentary Affairs, Honourable Ziyambi Ziyambi, brought together Cabinet ministers, senior Government officials, development partners, civil society organisations, health experts and representatives of the intersex community.
The process follows a legal challenge that exposed gaps in Zimbabwe’s existing legal framework, which currently recognises only male and female sex classifications. In response, the Ministry of Justice tasked the Law Development Commission, with support from the United Nations Development Programme (UNDP), to undertake research and national consultations on the legal and social challenges experienced by intersex persons. The consultations identified barriers arising from the absence of appropriate legal recognition, including difficulties in obtaining birth certificates, national identity documents and other official records, as well as resulting challenges in accessing education, healthcare, banking services, employment and voter registration. They also highlighted concerns relating to stigma and discrimination, bodily autonomy, non-consensual medical interventions involving intersex children, and limited awareness among service providers.
Minister Ziyambi indicated that Government intends to use the research findings, stakeholder inputs and testimonies to develop a coordinated, whole-of-Government and whole-of-society response and ultimately propose concrete policy and legislative measures. The development therefore represents an important step towards addressing longstanding legal and administrative barriers affecting intersex persons and strengthening their recognition, dignity and access to fundamental rights and public services in Zimbabwe.

Title: Sentencing of Malian journalist Chahana Takiou for critique of the use of Cybercrimes Bill
Content:
On 3 August 2026, the National Cybercrime Unit in Bamako sentenced the Malian journalist Chahana Takiou, editor-in-chief of the bi-weekly newspaper Le 22 Septembre, to twelve months’ imprisonment, six months to be served and six months suspended, along with a fine of 500,000 FCFA. He was prosecuted for “undermining the State’s credibility through the judicial system”, after criticising, at the Pan-African Media Forum held in Bamako in early June 2026, the use of the cybercrime law rather than the press offences regime to try a fellow journalist.
Placed under a remand order on 8 June 2026, he spent nearly two months in pre-trial detention ahead of his trial, despite a request for provisional release on health grounds being rejected by the public prosecutor’s office. The journalist decided not to appeal against this decision to the Court of Appeal, the court of second instance. His release, following the completion of his custodial sentence, is due to take place on 8 December 2026, unless a presidential pardon is granted before that date.
Reporters Without Borders has condemned an arbitrary detention that forms part of a continuing deterioration in the conditions under which the press operates during the current transition. The Malian Press Association has stated that these proceedings tarnish the image of the judiciary, the press and the country. This condemnation is the latest in a series of prosecutions targeting Malian journalists and reinforces concerns that cybercrime legislation is being used to restrict press freedom and pluralism in public debate in Mali.

Title: Court acquits GALA members, affirming protections for peaceful assembly
Content:
On 9 July 2026, the Banjul Magistrates’ Court acquitted members of the civil society movement Gambians Against Looted Assets (GALA) who had been prosecuted on charges of unlawful assembly following a protest outside the National Audit Office (NAO) in September 2025. In a ruling delivered by Principal Magistrate Sallah Mbye, the court held that the prosecution had failed to establish that the gathering met the legal threshold for an unlawful assembly and ruled that the accused had no case to answer.
The case arose after GALA members organised a protest opposing the removal of the Auditor General, arguing that the decision undermined the independence of the National Audit Office and public accountability. The acquittal has been widely welcomed by civil society as an important affirmation of due process and judicial independence. The judgment also reinforces constitutional protections for peaceful assembly by demonstrating that criminal charges against protesters must be supported by sufficient evidence rather than assumptions arising from civic mobilisation. At the same time, the case highlights the continuing use of criminal proceedings against civic activists, even where prosecutions ultimately fail, illustrating how lengthy legal processes can themselves impose costs on civil society participation.

Title: Tax Administration Act takes effect with mixed implications for civil society
Content:
Botswana has recently implemented the Tax Administration Act, 2026, a key piece of legislation that has significant implications for the civil society enabling environment. The legislative development introduces important changes to the regulatory and operational context within which civil society organisations (CSOs) operate, with potential impacts on organisational sustainability, compliance, governance, and human resource practices.
The Tax Administration Act, 2026, which came into effect on 1 July 2026 alongside the re-enacted Income Tax Act, Value Added Tax (VAT) Act, and Customs Act, forms part of broader government efforts to modernise tax administration, improve revenue collection, and strengthen public financial management. The reform process included stakeholder engagement providing an opportunity for CSOs and other stakeholders to contribute to discussions on the new framework. While the reforms are intended to strengthen accountability and efficiency in tax administration, they also introduce new compliance requirements that may affect CSOs. Organisations may need to enhance their financial management, accounting, and tax administration systems, with smaller and community-based organisations potentially facing greater challenges due to limited resources and technical capacity. Ensuring access to guidance, capacity building, and proportionate compliance measures will be important to maintain an enabling environment for civil society.
This legislative development demonstrate progress in strengthening regulatory frameworks that influence the operating environment for CSOs. However, effective implementation will require continued government–civil society dialogue, clear guidance, and targeted support to enable organisations, particularly smaller CSOs, to comply with new requirements while continuing to deliver essential services and contribute to national development.

Title: Government invites civil society submissions on National Policing Bill
Content:
On 3 August 2026, the Federal Government’s launched a seven-week roadmap for developing the proposed National Policing Bill. The Presidential Working Group, chaired by Chief of Staff Femi Gbajabiamila, is expected to work from 27 July to 14 September 2026 on a framework for state police, national minimum policing standards, state readiness and certification, recruitment, training, oversight, funding, and accountability. Nigerians, civil society organisations, professional bodies, and other stakeholders have been invited to submit memoranda and policy proposals through the government’s online submission portal during a two-week public-input window. The draft Executive Bill is expected to be presented to President Bola Ahmed Tinubu on 3 September 2026.
The roadmap launch takes place within Nigeria’s continuing debate over the creation of state police and the decentralisation of internal security. The proposed framework is expected to address national minimum policing standards, state readiness and certification, recruitment, training, funding, oversight, accountability, and coordination between federal and state police services. The process is significant because it could reshape policing responsibilities across Nigeria while also raising concerns about political interference, human-rights protection, command structures, and safeguards against abuse of state police powers.
Before the public consultation closes on 13 August 2026, civil society organisations should prepare and submit evidence-based memoranda, drawing on consultations with affected communities and closely monitoring whether the consultation process remains inclusive, participatory and transparent. Civil society should also coordinate a joint position paper that highlights key safeguards, including the protection of human rights, independent complaints and accountability mechanisms, effective civilian oversight, safeguards against political interference, gender-responsive policing, robust data protection measures, and clear delineation of federal and state policing responsibilities.
In addition, civil society should establish an independent monitoring mechanism to track public submissions, proposed amendments and implementation commitments throughout the reform process. This mechanism should document any instances of intimidation, harassment or abuse associated with the reform and produce accessible public briefings that keep citizens informed of developments. Collectively, these actions would help ensure that state policing reforms enhance public safety, accountability and respect for human rights, rather than creating opportunities for abuse or political repression.

Title: State governments, church bodies and civil society mobilize against the proposed FCRA Amendment Bill, 2026
Content:
Through July 2026, a series of state-level and civil-society interventions signalled growing opposition to the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Amendment Bill, 2026, particularly its asset-related provisions.
On 1 July 2026, the Kerala Legislative Assembly passed a resolution demanding that the Central Government withdraw its move to amend the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act. Chief Minister V. D. Satheesan stated that the proposed modification went against the spirit of the resolution and could not be accepted, and rejected a demand by BJP MLA V. Muraleedharan to modify it. The resolution was passed with dissent from BJP MLAs B. B. Gopakumar and V. Muraleedharan. It noted that the Central Government’s FCRA directives would adversely affect the smooth functioning of voluntary and charitable institutions working in the social, health, educational and charitable sectors — organisations that significantly support government mechanisms in areas such as the welfare of marginalised communities, education, healthcare, medical aid for the destitute, rehabilitation of the differently-abled, and disaster management.
On 5 July 2026, a delegation led by Meghalaya Chief Minister Conrad K. Sangma met Union Home Minister Amit Shah to express concerns over the proposed amendment, particularly Section 16A(5), which would allow authorities to take over or dispose of assets created through foreign contributions if an organisation’s FCRA registration is cancelled or not renewed. The delegation highlighted that faith-based and charitable organisations have long supported education, healthcare and community development in Meghalaya, especially in remote areas, and urged the Centre to adopt a consultative approach with adequate safeguards.
On 11 July 2026, the Nagaland Baptist Church Council (NBCC) urged Chief Minister Neiphiu Rio to press the Central Government to withdraw the proposed Bill, arguing that it could adversely affect churches, faith-based organisations, charitable institutions and civil society groups engaged in humanitarian and development work. The NBCC — representing 21 Baptist Associations, 1,626 congregations and over 748,000 baptised members — warned that the amendments could increase regulatory burdens, disrupt humanitarian programmes, discourage international partnerships, and enable the takeover of assets if FCRA registrations are cancelled. It appealed to the Nagaland Government to adopt a position similar to the Kerala Assembly and called for a broad-based consultative process involving state governments, churches, faith-based organisations, civil society groups and development agencies before any amendments are enacted.
The appeals from state assemblies, state governments and church bodies constitute an opportunity for broader pushback against the amendment and signal responsiveness of these state governments to civil society concern. They also highlight the continuing need for broader consultation with faith-based organisations and civil society before finalising legislative changes.

Title: ICRC representative conducts rare private visit with detained State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi as junta continues to deny legal access
Content:
On 3 August 2026, the Myanmar military junta announced that Arnaud de Baecque, Resident Representative of the International Committee of the Red Cross (ICRC) to Myanmar, met with detained State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi in Naypyidaw. The junta publicized state photographs of the meeting while withholding specific details regarding her precise physical location or health condition.
The Assistance Association for Political Prisoners (AAPP) heavily criticized the regime, emphasizing that selective access granted exclusively to the ICRC underscores that the junta continues to treat the democratically elected leader merely as a high-value prisoner. The AAPP reiterated demands for her immediate, unconditional release and the recognition of her legitimate leadership role to resolve the national crisis.
On the evening of 3 August, the ICRC formally confirmed the visit, noting that it was conducted under its standard humanitarian procedures for individuals deprived of liberty, which included an unmonitored private conversation. This marks her first confirmed meeting with an international delegation since her transfer to an undisclosed location in late April 2026.

Title: Presidential administration official publishes personal data of civil society actors and threatens critics with arrest
Content:
On 20 July 2026, the Head of the Information Policy Service of the Presidential Administration published a Facebook post accusing groups of social media users of spreading false information and “anti-China” narratives. The post included collages showing names, dates of birth, social media accounts and photographs of civil society representatives, journalists, human rights defenders, political commentators and activists. The official warned that those who continued such activity could be identified, detained and imprisoned.

Media reports noted that the original post grouped individuals according to alleged links with opposition figures and civil society organisations (CSOs). Several people included in the collages also reportedly observed that some photographs had never been publicly available and appeared to match ID photographs stored in the state “Tunduk” system. This raised concerns about possible unauthorised access to and use of state-held personal data. As of 22 July, the authorities had not publicly explained the source of the photographs. In response, lawyer Nurbek Toktakunov issued an open appeal to President Sadyr Japarov, requesting an independent investigation into the possible misuse of personal data and an assessment of whether Orunbekov’s statements breached civil service standards.

The incident raises serious concerns about freedom of expression, digital privacy and the safety of civil society actors. By publicly targeting individuals engaged in legitimate criticism and advocacy, it risks creating a climate of intimidation and self-censorship that undermines civic participation and further restricts the enabling environment for civil society.

Title: Use of force by police to disperse protesters at the National University of Ucayali leave students injured
Content:
On the night of 6 July, police officers and students at the National University of Ucayali (UNU) clashed during a new round of protests. Following a meeting of the University Council, a group of demonstrators attempted to intercept the Rector and reiterate their demand for his resignation. In response, a police contingent entered the university to provide security for the Rector.
According to the testimony of a student, an initial group of 16 police officers arrived at the campus, prompting students to form a human chain to prevent their entry. However, several hours later, a larger police contingent returned and entered the university, triggering clashes with the protesters. The Rector reportedly left the campus disguised as a police officer to avoid the demonstrators.
During the operation, police used tear gas and physical force to disperse the protesters, while students responded with shouting and pushing. Student representatives also alleged that “police officers posed as students in order to provoke unrest”. The police intervention left at least ten students injured, suffering bruises and multiple contusions.
The Federation of Students of the National University of Ucayali (FEUNU) has called for an investigation into the police intervention and for those responsible for the alleged excessive use of force to be identified. The federation also urged the Ombudsman's Office, the Public Prosecutor's Office, the Judiciary, and the National Police to guarantee students' fundamental rights and protect public higher education.
Several organizations condemned the police response. The National Human Rights Coordinator (CNDDHH) denounced the police repression, while the Manuela Ramos Movement, several university federations, and the PUCP Alumni Front also rejected the violence. In addition, the Lima Bar Association called on the Ucayali Bar Association to provide legal assistance to the affected students.

Title: Some lawmakers from parties in the governing coalition have introduced a bill that would require women to listen to the fetal heartbeat before undergoing an abortion under any of the three grounds established by law
Content:
On 7 July 206 members of Congress from the National Libertarian Party, the Republican Party, and National Renewal introduced the "Listen to Her Heartbeat" bill (Bill 18419-11), which would require doctors to offer women seeking abortions under the three legal grounds (rape, fetal inviability, or risk to the mother's life) the option of listening to the embryo's heartbeat electronically. The bill stipulates that if a woman refuses this option, the doctor must refuse to perform the abortion.
The bill has generated widespread condemnation from civil society organizations specializing in sexual and reproductive rights, former ministers, the Chilean Medical Association, and other healthcare professionals, who describe the initiative as another form of obstetric violence that could exacerbate the suffering of already vulnerable women and girls. The Circle of Studies on International Human Rights Law points out that the bill's rationale directly contradicts Chile's obligations to protect women from violence and discrimination in the healthcare sector.
Meanwhile, more than 50 civil society organizations, along with feminist groups, have called for a national protest in various cities across the country. They are also concerned that the initiative spearheaded by Congressman Cristobal Urruticoechea has already passed its first constitutional hurdle, in a context where the committees that will review the bill in the future are controlled by the ruling party.

Title: Kinshasa: crackdown on doctors’ sit-in outside a government building
Content: On 14 July 2026, a collective of doctors not receiving hazard pay organised a sit-in outside the Government House in Kinshasa to demand that they be brought into line with the hazard pay scheme, the regular payment of salaries, and the regularisation of the status of unpaid doctors. Whilst they were demonstrating in the hope of being received by the Minister of Health to present their grievances, members of the Congolese National Police brutalised them, hosed them down with water to disperse them, and one doctor was even beaten up.

Title: New law allows on military courts for service-related offences raises accountability concerns
Content:
On 21 July, Law No. 32735, the Law Amending the Military and Police Criminal Code (Legislative Decree No. 1094) and the New Criminal Procedure Code (Legislative Decree No. 957) was enacted. The law aims to clarify the definition of service-related offences, strengthen the role of the military and police, and establish sanctions for military and police personnel involved in criminal gangs or organizations.
Among the provisions that could adversely affect the enabling environment are the following:

Any unlawful conduct committed by police officers or military personnel—including homicide, corruption, human rights violations, and property-related offences—in areas under a state of emergency may be tried by military courts.
Human life is not a military legal interest protected under military jurisdiction. Homicide affects a general legal interest, and this does not change simply because the perpetrator used service weapons or exercised powers derived from official duties. Such circumstances may aggravate an ordinary criminal offence, but they do not transform it into a military one.

This law could facilitate impunity in cases involving human rights violations or acts of corruption committed in alignment with military or government superiors. It also revives associations between the military justice system and some of the darkest legacies of Peru's authoritarian and corrupt governments. According to OjoPúblico, more than 80 ongoing investigations could be transferred to the military and police courts following the enactment of this law.
Following its publication, a press conference was held at the Lima Bar Association, convened by relatives of victims of human rights violations committed during the Internal Armed Conflict (1980–2000), the 2020 social protests, the 2022–2023 massacres, and cases of state violence in 2025–2026, together with the National Human Rights Coordinator (CNDDHH), to denounce legislation aimed at guaranteeing impunity. The CNDDHH and Amnesty International Peru have also publicly rejected this law and other related legislative initiatives. On 23 July, the "Plantón 50" demonstration was held outside the Palace of Justice, organised by the No + Impunidad ("No More Impunity") collective.
In the legal arena, an opposition member of Congress has introduced a bill to repeal Law No. 32735 and has called on the newly elected members of Congress to reopen consideration of the proposal and give it priority during the next legislative session. Meanwhile, the Cusco Bar Association has filed a partial constitutional complaint before the Constitutional Court, seeking to have several provisions of the law declared unconstitutional.
