Respect and protection: Accountability for human rights violations

Title: Administrative harassment and selective enforcement against pro-democracy businesses
Content:
On 3 August 2026, the retail shop and group-buying platform "As One" (如一), operated by former pro-democracy District Councillor Chu Kong-wai, was forced by the Buildings Department to demolish its shop signs, raised floor, and air-conditioning units over alleged unauthorized building works. Mundane checks are weaponized to target and financially exhaust civic spaces. While neighboring shops on Tai Nan Street in Prince Edward were also issued demolition orders, Chu noted that the speed of enforcement was unprecedented: they received court summonses shortly after the initial orders, forcing them to conduct disruptive construction works just before the crucial Mid-Autumn Festival sales period.
This mirrors an established pattern of sustained administrative harassment against pro-democracy ("yellow") businesses. For instance, in September 2025, the well-known "yellow" eatery Keelung Restaurant (基隆茶餐廳) was abruptly ordered to remove its 20-year-old shopfront sign as an "illegal structure" following anonymous complaints. The restaurant's owner reported that since April 2025, they had faced an exhausting barrage of inspections from multiple government departments, including the Food and Environmental Hygiene Department and the Fire Services Department, who admitted they were responding to external complaints.

Title: Politically motivated dismissal of activist dentist and systemic harassment via employers
Content:
In late July 2026, Lee Ying-chi, a dentist and known activist, was summarily dismissed from her clinic, a non-profit organisation with government partnerships, shortly after staging a peaceful solo demonstration on the anniversary of the 2019 Yuen Long mob attack (21 July). During the protest, Lee held a watermelon and a photo of a prominent, unprosecuted attacker from 2019 (known as "Watermelon Man") and was stopped and searched by police. Three days after this widely reported incident, clinic management pressured her to resign.
Human Resources claimed she had failed to declare a past fine for "unlicensed fundraising," but explicitly stated that retaining her would jeopardise the organisation's "partnership with the government," asking her to "sympathise with their situation." When Lee refused to resign voluntarily, asserting she had never let her activism interfere with her professional duties or work hours, she was fired with immediate effect. She was barred from packing her personal belongings and crucially, prevented from properly handing over her patients' clinical care. Therefore, demonstrating a systemic pattern of harassment designed to economically and socially isolate civil society actors.

Title: Government Shuts Down Special Unit Created to Investigate Illegal Adoptions During the Dictatorship
Content:

Although the Undersecretary of Human Rights assures that the work will continue under its purview, civil society organizations working on human rights and former officials in the field describe the decision as a “step backward for the state” that leaves thousands of cases of irregular adoptions in limbo and halts the creation of a DNA database.

Title: The Committee of Ministers rejected the appeals filed by civil society against the Mataquito mega-electric project

Title: Arbitrary arrest, and alleged sexual violence against members of Al-Wehda Emergency Room – North Kordofan
Content:
On Monday, 23 June 2026, three members of Al-Wehda Emergency Room in El Obeid, North Kordofan, Sudan, were arrested by a force affiliated with the General Intelligence Service. The three members, including a female volunteer, were detained for approximately two days before being released. During the detention period, the detainees reported being subjected to physical assault and ill-treatment. According to the survivors’ testimonies, while one female volunteer was taken separately for interrogation and questioning by members of the security apparatus, another female volunteer who remained in detention was allegedly subjected to rape by two individuals affiliated with the General Intelligence Service. It is believed that the sexual violence may have been linked to her ethnic background, particularly in the context of recent accusations and labeling of certain ethnic groups as “social bases/supporters of the Rapid Support Forces (RSF).” This allegation requires further investigation and verification to establish the motive behind the attack.
The security forces also reportedly searched the detainees’ personal phones and accessed their private information. The detainees stated that their arrest was based on accusations of cooperation with the Rapid Support Forces (RSF) and communication with civil and political actors. Following their release, they were reportedly forced to sign undertakings requiring them to report weekly to the offices of the General Intelligence Service and were informed that they would remain under continuous security surveillance. The reported violations include arbitrary detention, physical abuse and ill-treatment during detention, alleged conflict-related sexual violence, violation of privacy, coercion, restrictions on civic activities, and intimidation of humanitarian and civil society actor

Title: Extended social media blackout in Gabon: WhatsApp accounts hacked in connection with the use of VPN
Content:
For several weeks since the end of June 2026, Gabon has been facing a surge in cybercrime ; many users have reported that their personal and work WhatsApp accounts have been hacked, including the WhatsApp group for the editorial team of the national television channel Gabon Télévision. This situation has prompted a coalition of civil society organisations to call for the lifting of the social media ban, which has been in place for over five months.
It should be noted that following the announcement of the social media ban with immediate effect on 17 February 2026, Gabonese people automatically began using VPNs to circumvent the ban, but these new methods of connecting to the internet are not without consequences: civil society organisations have already recorded around fifty complaints regarding the hacking of personal and professional WhatsApp accounts. This phenomenon illustrates the adverse effects of a prolonged suspension of social media: rather than protecting the digital space, it leaves users even more vulnerable to cyberattacks.

Title: Harassment and surveillance of TISA and members of the Okoa Uchumi Campaign
Content:
Since early June 2026, the Executive Director of the Institute for Social Accountability (TISA) has reportedly been subjected to a sustained pattern of intrusive surveillance and road harassment, including repeated tailing along routes she regularly uses to and from work. On 2 July 2026, at least 13 individuals alleged to be state security officers reportedly attempted to gain entry into TISA's offices without following lawful procedures. Civil society organisations have further alleged that these incidents form part of a broader, coordinated campaign of intimidation targeting TISA, its Executive Director, staff members and other participants in the Okoa Uchumi Campaign.
In response to these developments, a coalition of civil society organisations issued a joint press statement on 13 July 2026 condemning what it described as police intimidation of activists and an organised, state-enabled campaign of terror against citizens exercising their constitutional rights. The statement called for investigations into the alleged surveillance, harassment, and attempted raid on TISA's offices, as well as broader protections for civic actors.
These reported incidents point to a further deterioration of Kenya's civic space and enabling environment for civil society. Such allegations of surveillance, intimidation, and harassment against civil society actors have a chilling effect on civic participation, freedom of association and the ability of civil society organisations to undertake accountability and public interest work without fear of reprisals.

Title: Activist Sentenced to 30 Days in Prison Over a Social Media Post
Content:
On 27 July 2026, activist Gabriela Panchana Briones was sentenced to 30 days in prison and ordered to issue a public apology for a post published on the social media platform X. According to a statement issued by Panchana, the sentence resulted from a complaint filed by another user of the platform under Article 396 of Ecuador's Organic Comprehensive Criminal Code (COIP), which penalizes expressions deemed to dishonor or discredit another person. The activist maintained that the post in question did not refer to any specific individual. In addition, during the legal proceedings, organizations such as Fundamedios reported that they were denied access to the hearing, despite its public nature and the fact that it was conducted remotely.
The existence and enforcement of Article 396 of the COIP constitute an obstacle to the full enjoyment of freedom of expression in Ecuador and are inconsistent with the Inter-American human rights standards to which the Ecuadorian State has committed itself. Furthermore, restrictions on access to a public hearing undermine the principles of transparency and openness in the administration of justice, limiting the ability of civil society organizations to monitor judicial proceedings of public interest.
The Comité Permanente por la Defensa de los Derechos Humanos (CDH) and other civil society organizations condemned both the sentence and the restrictions on access to the hearings, warning that the criminal justice system may be used to discourage the exercise of freedom of expression and dissent, particularly against individuals who are critical of the government of President Daniel Noboa.

Title: Judicial proceedings and police summonses of journalists following the publication of a report on the forced eviction of “Koumassi Campement” in Abidjan, Côte d’Ivoire.
Content:
On 8 July 2026, the online news outlet L’Éléphant Déchaîné published an investigative report on the controversial eviction of residents from the Koumassi Campement neighborhood in Abidjan. In response, the Governor of the Autonomous District of Abidjan, Cissé Bacongo, initiated a series of actions directly targeting the newspaper's editorial team. On 13 July, he sent the outlet a right of reply together with a formal notice demanding that it produce evidence within 48 hours, under the threat of legal proceedings. Considering this demand to be contrary to Article 71 of the Press Law, the newspaper referred the matter to the National Press Authority (ANP) on 14 July.
However, the governor followed through on his threat by filing a criminal complaint with the Public Prosecutor. Acting on the prosecutor's instructions, the Abidjan Police Prefecture summoned the two journalists responsible for the publication, Tiemoko Antoine Assale and Stéphane Bahi, for questioning scheduled for Monday, 3 August 2026. This development marks an unprecedented escalation in the use of the judicial and police apparatus to pressure an investigative media outlet.

Title: Alleged administrative reprisals against USAC students raise concerns over the right to education and civic space
Content:
Between 20 and 24 July 2026, at least 40 students from different faculties and regional campuses of the University of San Carlos of Guatemala (USAC) reported that their academic records had disappeared from the Department of Registration and Statistics system, preventing them from enrolling for the academic term and continuing their studies. The affected students state that they were not notified of any administrative procedure or decision justifying the removal of their records and therefore consider that their rights to education and due process have been violated.
The students argue that the measure constitutes retaliation against those who have expressed critical views of the administration of Rector Walter Mazariegos, whose elections in 2022 and 2026 were widely questioned due to allegations of irregularities. In this context, they describe the disappearance of their academic records as a form of "academic death," as it prevents them from continuing their university education. They also reported that several affected students have chosen not to speak publicly about their situation for fear of further reprisals.
In response, the students submitted formal petitions to the Department of Registration and Statistics requesting the restoration of their academic records and an official explanation. At the same time, the Human Rights Ombudsman's Office (PDH) opened an investigation, provided support to the affected students, and initiated proceedings to assess possible violations of the right to education and other legal guarantees. In addition, a complaint was filed with the Public Prosecutor's Office requesting an investigation into the alleged removal or destruction of academic records.
The reported incidents have raised concerns among students and human rights organisations due to their potential implications for the right to education, freedom of expression, and student participation. They also raise concerns about the conditions for exercising these rights and the functioning of civic space within the country's only public university. The perception of possible administrative reprisals against people who express critical positions could discourage denunciation, collective organization, participation in university spaces and the defense of rights, affecting the civic space within the university and limiting the role of the USAC as a space for plural debate and citizen training.

Title: Colombia officially launches the National Action Plan on Human Rights 2026–2036
Content:
The National Government officially launched the National Action Plan on Human Rights (PNADH) 2026–2036, a long-term public policy adopted through Decree 0585 of 5 June 2026. The official launch took place on 15 July 2026 and was led by the Presidential Office for Human Rights, with the participation of government agencies, international organizations, labor unions, and representatives of civil society.
The Plan establishes a roadmap for the next ten years with nearly 200 strategic actions aimed at strengthening the promotion, protection, and guarantee of human rights in Colombia. Its objectives include consolidating human rights institutions, strengthening citizen participation, preventing human rights violations, protecting particularly vulnerable populations, and fostering coordination among national and regional entities. The document incorporates differential, territorial, ethnic, gender, and intersectional approaches.
The Plan is presented as a state policy that seeks to transcend individual administrations and fulfill national and international commitments regarding human rights, including recommendations from international mechanisms and commitments arising from the Final Peace Agreement. Given that the plan is currently under the Presidential Office for Human Rights and the incoming government has announced that this office will be dissolved, it is expected that responsibility for its implementation will be transferred to an entity that assumes those responsibilities, such as the Ministry of the Interior. According to the agency’s announcement, although the decree has been issued, the task of developing the indicators and disseminating them nationwide, particularly to local governments, which will play a central role in their implementation, remains pending.

Title: Withdrawal of the Republic of Chad from the Rome Statute of the ICC
Content:
On 27 July 2026, the Government of the Republic of Chad notified the Secretary-General of the United Nations, the depositary of the Rome Statute, of its sovereign decision to withdraw from the International Criminal Court (ICC), in accordance with Article 127 of the Rome Statute. This announcement was formalized in an official statement from the Chadian Ministry of Foreign Affairs, signed by spokesperson Ibrahim Adam Mahamat.
Chad justifies its decision by pointing to what it considers an unbalanced track record of the Court since its creation in 2002: of the 13 investigations opened, 9 involve African states, compared with only 4 in other regions, and of the 7 individuals currently detained by the ICC, 6 are being held in connection with situations in Africa. N'Djamena sees this as a sign of the Court’s “political manipulation” and presents this withdrawal as an act to defend its sovereignty. The country is calling on the African Union to strengthen African judicial mechanisms in order to build a more equitable continental justice system, while reaffirming its commitment to combating impunity for serious crimes.
This withdrawal echoes the stance already taken by Mali and Burkina Faso, two member countries of the Alliance of Sahel States (AES), which also accuse the ICC of bias. In accordance with Article 127, the withdrawal will not take effect for another year, on 27 July 2027; until then, Chad remains bound by its obligations, and the Court retains jurisdiction over crimes committed prior to that date. The ICC has thus lost a third African country in less than two years, reigniting the debate over its presence on the continent.

Title: Civil society and public stakeholders call on Trinidad and Tobago to resist US pressure against the ICC and associated organisations
Content:
On 13 July 2026, the United States announced a campaign to dismantle or systematically disable the International Criminal Court (ICC). The measures reportedly include diplomatic pressure on ICC States Parties, possible reductions in assistance, additional financial sanctions, visa restrictions and efforts to persuade countries to withdraw political and financial support from the Court. Trinidad and Tobago is particularly affected because it is a longstanding ICC State Party and played a formative role in the Court’s establishment through the advocacy of former prime minister and president Arthur NR Robinson.
The announcement prompted public intervention from stakeholders in Trinidad and Tobago. Movement for Social Justice leader David Abdulah urged the Government not to support the United States initiative; Independent Senator Anthony Vieira argued that silence was not an acceptable response; and former minister Winston Dookeran warned that weakening the Court would undermine international accountability. Former foreign affairs minister Dr Amery Browne also called for the Government to disclose its position. However, Prime Minister Kamla Persad-Bissessar initially declined to comment publicly on the campaign.
The event affects civil society’s enabling environment because organisations supporting international justice, victims and human-rights accountability have already been targeted by United States sanctions. Further escalation could discourage Trinidad and Tobago organisations from engaging with the ICC, constrain funding and banking access, and create fear of travel, financial or reputational consequences. At the same time, the open interventions by domestic stakeholders and media demonstrate continuing space for civic advocacy. The key concern is whether this advocacy receives a transparent and responsive government answer.

Title: Preventive detention order review prompts civil society calls for system-wide oversight and equal access to justice
Content:
Between 23 and 26 July 2026, legal professionals and civil-society actors responded to the Government’s decision to revoke the Preventive Detention Orders issued against business owners Dominic and Genevieve Hadeed during Trinidad and Tobago’s continuing State of Emergency. The Ministry of Homeland Security stated that the decision followed a review of the legal, medical and public-interest considerations surrounding the case, as well as recommendations from the relevant review tribunal. Saira Lakhan, president of the Assembly of Southern Lawyers, welcomed the decision and stated that it demonstrated the need for emergency powers to remain under continuous review and to be exercised lawfully, necessarily and proportionately. She also cautioned that the continuing criminal investigation should be allowed to proceed through due process.
Other legal advocates called for the same scrutiny and access to representation to be extended to less prominent detainees. Former House Speaker Nizam Mohammed urged attorneys to form a consortium to represent people detained under PDOs who cannot afford legal assistance, particularly those from economically disadvantaged communities. Separately, former attorney general Ramesh Lawrence Maharaj questioned whether regulations allowing a government minister to determine continued detention improperly transfer judicial functions to the executive. The development constitutes a limited positive response to concerns about emergency detention, demonstrating that review mechanisms can result in corrective action, while highlighting that broader transparency, oversight and access-to-justice concerns remain unresolved.

Title: Civil society calls for risk-based assessment of non-profit sector during drafting of the proposed Non-Profit Organisations Act
Content:
On 22 July 2026, the Council of Voluntary Social Services (CVSS) publicly called on the Government of Jamaica to undertake a comprehensive assessment of the money laundering and terrorist financing risks associated with the non-profit sector as part of the development of the proposed Non-Profit Organisations (NPO) Act. During the Let's Talk Justice programme, produced by Jamaicans for Justice and aired on Nationwide 90FM, CVSS Executive Director Nancy Pinchas argued that the proposed legislative framework should be informed by an evidence-based risk assessment rather than imposing uniform compliance obligations on all non-profit organisations.
The CVSS expressed concern that existing anti-money laundering and counter-terrorism financing requirements under the Charities Act have already created significant administrative burdens for charities and community-based organisations. Stakeholders also reiterated concerns regarding limited opportunities for meaningful participation in the legislative drafting process and emphasised that the experiences and recommendations of the non-profit sector should inform the development of the new regulatory framework before it is finalised.

Title: Persecution of Political Opponents and Alleged Subversive Military Figures: An Ongoing Reality in Guinea-Bissau
Content:
Since the coup d'état of 23 November 2025, the leader of the PAIGC, Engineer Domingos Simões Pereira, has remained under intense political persecution by the regime, in an apparent attempt to prevent him from carrying out political activities through the use of the judicial system. He was placed under house arrest on 31 January 2026 after being released from prison, where he had been detained following the military coup of 26 November 2025. On Friday, 10 July 2026, he was transferred to the cells of the Second Public Order Police Station in Bissau by order of the Investigating Judge. He subsequently left the country to receive medical treatment and arrived in Lisbon, Portugal, in the early hours of 24 July.
The case of General Daba Na Walna remains ongoing and reflects the political and military persecution taking place in Guinea-Bissau. The Supreme Court overturned the general's pretrial detention order, but the same Investigating Judge subsequently reversed that decision, creating a legal deadlock and maintaining pressure on opposition figures and military personnel accused of subversion.
On the other hand, Mr. Carlitos Costa, a senior PAIGC official, was abducted, beaten, and abandoned on the night of Saturday, 25 July 2026, at around 10:00 p.m., by five armed, masked individuals. His assault is directly linked to his opposition to the constitutional referendum scheduled for 30 August 2026. Shortly before the attack, he had broadcast a live video on social media urging citizens to vote "No," which was interpreted as a challenge to the transitional authorities.

Title: Senate Introduction of Foreign Aid and NGO Oversight Bill
Content:
During a plenary session on 22 July 2026, the Senate passed for second reading a bill sponsored by Senator Ibrahim Hassan Dankwambo that seeks to establish a National Donor Coordination Framework and mandate compulsory registration of all foreign aid and donor‑funded projects with the federal government. Entitled ‘A Bill for an Act to Provide for the Regulation, Coordination, Transparency and Disclosure of Foreign Aid, Grants and Donations in the Federal Republic of Nigeria, 2026 (SB. 10340)’, the Senator argued that the bill was supported by constitutional provisions on legislative oversight for public funds and that foreign aid deployed to Nigeria should be treated as such. The proposed law would create a national database of foreign assistance, require that donor‑funded interventions be integrated into national planning and budgeting processes, and impose mandatory public disclosure of funding sources and project implementation details.
Lawmakers justified the move by citing concerns about weak transparency, fragmented oversight, and possible national security risks associated with unregulated foreign aid flows, especially through NGOs and sub‑national entities. This is in line with previous narratives by lawmakers alleging that foreign aid is used to fund Boko Haram, including an investigation into USAID funding in 2025.  After debate, the Senate referred the bill to the relevant committees on National Planning and Economic Development, Finance, and in some accounts Foreign Affairs for further legislative work and public hearings, with a directive that they report back within four to six weeks.
By centralising control over all foreign aid and donor‑funded projects in a mandatory registration and national database system, the bill would significantly reshape the legal framework and conditions under which NGOs and other actors can receive and use foreign funding, increasing state discretion and compliance burdens. This directly affects civil society’s access to resources and limits operational freedoms, especially in an already restrictive and over‑regulated context for Nigerian civil society. NGOs, development partners and government agencies would all be covered by the new regime, but independent and rights‑based CSOs are likely to feel the greatest pressure, as funding oversight can easily be used to discourage critical advocacy or steer resources towards government‑aligned priorities. Over time, such a framework can lead to large‑scale, systemic change by normalising tighter control over civil society financing, changing who gets funded and what issues are deemed acceptable, and setting a precedent for further restrictive measures justified in the name of transparency and national security.

Title: Arrest warrants issued against 47 Sudanese journalists
Content:
On Tuesday, 21 July 2026, Sudan’s Public Prosecution Office for Information Technology Crimes in the Red Sea State issued arrest warrants against more than 47 Sudanese journalists and media professionals, including newspaper editors-in-chief, online media supervisors, and media company officials. The authorities also listed the journalists as “fugitive accused persons” and gave those named one week from the date of publication to surrender to the nearest police station to complete legal procedures related to the case.
The first batch of published notices included prominent media figures such as Mohamed Abdelgadir, former adviser to the Prime Minister and editor-in-chief of Al-Karama newspaper; Muzdalifa Mohamed Osman, editor-in-chief of Sudan Tribune; Alwaleed Fait Mohamed Ahmed, director of Noon International; and Mohamed Ahmed Khidr Tabidi, editor-in-chief of Masarib Al-Dai newspaper. Additional notices and arrest warrants are reportedly expected to be published.
The Sudanese Journalists’ Network expressed concern over the measures and emphasized the presumption of innocence and the right to a fair trial, legal representation, and due process. It warned against using cybercrime laws to intimidate journalists or restrict press freedom, stressing that any restrictions on freedom of expression must be lawful, necessary, proportionate, and non-arbitrary. The Network also rejected describing journalists living abroad with known locations as “fugitives” and expressed solidarity with those affected.

Title: SpaceX enforces stricter Starlink Roam policies, triggering widespread internet disruptions and civil society pushback
Content:
SpaceX has imposed strict restrictions on Starlink terminals operating outside their country of registration, sparking severe concerns over widespread internet blackouts across Myanmar’s conflict zones. Under the updated Starlink Roam policy, which takes full effect on 17 August 2026, devices will function for only 30 consecutive days internationally unless users upgrade to a Priority Plan, localize their accounts, or return the hardware. Because Starlink is not officially authorized in Myanmar, tighter enforcement has already resulted in the deactivation of over 20 percent of active terminals inside the country.
While industry sources indicate the policy aims to combat cyber-scam syndicates operating along the Thai-Myanmar border, the crackdown has indiscriminately affected civilian and humanitarian communications in regions far from these scam centers, including Magway, Sagaing, and Arakan State. In response, a coalition of 255 civil society organizations (CSOs) submitted a joint appeal to SpaceX, the United States government, and international bodies. The coalition warned against the severe unintended consequences of blanket restrictions and urged SpaceX to adopt targeted enforcement using the documented geographic coordinates of scam compounds. Furthermore, they offered to collaborate with the company to establish a verification mechanism to protect legitimate humanitarian and civilian users.

Title: Adoption of a draft ordinance strengthening the revocation of citizenship: a worrying development for civil liberties and civic space
Content:
At a meeting of the Council of Ministers on 17 July 2026, chaired by General Assimi Goïta, the Government of Mali adopted a draft ordinance amending Act No. 2011-087 of 30 December 2011 on the Personal and Family Code, which governs, in particular, the loss and forfeiture of Malian nationality. Presented by the Minister for Justice and Human Rights, Keeper of the Seals, Mamoudou Kassogué, as a response to the shortcomings of the current system in the face of the ‘hostile actions’ of certain nationals, the reform extends revocation to Malians by birth, whereas this mechanism had previously been reserved, in almost all cases, for naturalised persons.
The new grounds include formal allegiance to another state, the use of former public office to harm Mali’s interests, holding a position of responsibility within a civil society organisation, a cooperative or a public-interest association, coupled with cooperation with entities classified as ‘hostile’ and pursuing secessionist or terrorist aims; exile combined with membership of a terrorist or separatist organisation; and acts of terrorism, the financing of terrorism or the glorification of terrorism. Deprivation of nationality may only be pronounced if it would render the person stateless. The text has so far only been adopted by the Government. Its promulgation by the President for it to come into force and its ratification by the legislature to ensure its long-term validity are still pending.

Title: Judicial dissolution of CNAPESTE and an attack on trade union luralism in Algeria
Content:
On 28 July 2026, the Bir Mourad Raïs Administrative Court in Algiers ordered the dissolution of the National Autonomous Council of Teaching Staff in the Tertiary Education Sector (CNAPESTE), an independent trade union recognised since 2007, and ordered the appointment of a liquidator. The proceedings had been initiated on 9 March 2026 by the Ministry of Labour, with the support of the Ministry of National Education, on the basis of Law No. 23-02 on the exercise of trade union rights, in particular on grounds relating to the compliance of the statutes and representativeness.
The trade union and its defence group maintain that they have fulfilled the necessary formalities and regard the proceedings as an attempt to neutralise independent trade union action. As the judgement is subject to provisional enforcement, the dissolution takes effect immediately, even if an appeal is lodged. This decision seriously undermines freedom of association, pluralism in the representation of workers and the ability of independent organisations to participate in social dialogue. Amnesty International has called for the immediate annulment of the judgement, whilst several political and civil society actors have denounced this as a major violation of trade union freedoms.

Title: Social Mobilizations and Civic Space Tensions During the FIFA World Cup 2026 in Mexico
Content:
During the weeks leading up to and following the opening of the 2026 FIFA World Cup, held on 11 June in Mexico City, various civil society groups took advantage of the international attention surrounding the tournament to highlight the country's longstanding structural challenges.
Among the most prominent were the mobilizations of the madres buscadoras ("searching mothers"), who organized marches and vigils to demand progress in investigations and draw attention to Mexico's ongoing crisis of enforced disappearances. At the same time, neighborhood organizations and urban collectives protested against the effects of gentrification, the displacement of residents and street vendors, and restrictions on the use of public spaces resulting from the security operations implemented in the host cities.
Although the demonstrations were largely peaceful and no pattern of widespread repression was documented, protests led by the National Coordinator of Education Workers (CNTE), including sit-ins and road blockades in the capital, heightened political tensions in the weeks preceding the tournament. Some incidents resulted in clashes between protesters and security forces, leaving several people injured.
Throughout June and July, the tournament in Mexico was characterized by a heavy police presence, mobility restrictions in strategic areas of the host cities (Mexico City, Guadalajara, and Monterrey), and government rhetoric questioning the legitimacy and motivations of some protest groups. These developments tested the exercise of fundamental freedoms in Mexico and highlighted the relationship between the Mexican state and organized civil society at a time when the country was under intense international scrutiny.

Title: Murder of Journalist Alejandro Leyva Aguilar Deepens Concerns over Freedom of Expression in Oaxaca
Content: On 22 July 2026, independent journalist Francisco Alejandro Leyva Aguilar was murdered in San Pablo Etla, Oaxaca, while at a restaurant near his home. Leyva was the author of the column El Zumbido del Moscardón ("The Horsefly's Buzz") and a frequent critic of the state administration, covering issues related to corruption, public security, and governance. Several national and international organizations, including ARTICLE 19, called on authorities to treat his journalistic work as the primary line of investigation, noting that the killing occurred amid escalating violence against the press in Mexico. The murder sparked demonstrations by citizens, family members, and journalists during the Guelaguetza—the state's most important cultural festival, held annually in July—who demanded justice, an independent investigation, and effective measures to ensure the protection of journalists and the exercise of freedom of expression.

Title: Junta proposes 43 constitutional amendments to systematically consolidate military power and disqualify democratic opposition
Content:
On 7 July 2026, junta leader Min Aung Hlaing submitted a message to the military-dominated parliament in Naypyidaw containing 43 proposed amendments to the military-drafted 2008 Constitution. The parliament formally recorded the receipt of the message but did not disclose the draft amendments or schedule a debate. The proposed changes fall under Articles 436(a) and 436(b). Because the military is constitutionally guaranteed 25 percent of parliamentary seats and the junta-proxy Union Solidarity and Development Party (USDP) dominates the legislature, the regime possesses the supermajority required to pass these amendments easily.
Leaked reports indicate that the junta aims to extend the restrictions of Article 59(f)—the clause historically used to bar State Counselor Aung San Suu Kyi from the presidency due to foreign family ties—to disqualify candidates for Union ministers and state or region chief ministers. The regime also reportedly plans to double the terms of the Constitutional Tribunal and the Union Election Commission (UEC) from five to ten years and will amend the constitution to allow UEC decisions to be appealed at the Supreme Court. Notably, the 43 points omitted a key demand from ethnic parties to revoke the president's authority to appoint state and region chief ministers, thereby rejecting calls to allow local legislatures to vote for their own leaders. Furthermore, the amendments modified Article 342, limiting the president's authority to appoint the Commander-in-Chief only to "when the post fell vacant," heavily insulating the current military leadership.

Title: Release of Journalists Zavqibek Saidamini and Abdusattor Pirmuhammadzoda
Content:
On 18 July 2026, independent journalists Zavqibek Saidamini and Abdusattor Pirmuhammadzoda were released from prison following the application of an amnesty law adopted in June 2026. Both journalists were sentenced to seven years of imprisonment in 2022 on charges related to their alleged participation in a banned organisation. Their convictions were widely criticised by civil society and international organisations as part of broader concerns regarding increasing restrictions on freedom of expression, media freedom, and the shrinking space for independent journalism in Tajikistan. 
On 26 December 2022, journalist and blogger Abdusattor Pirmukhammadzoda was sentenced by a Dushanbe court to seven years in prison following a closed trial. In autumn 2022, a handwritten letter from Pirmukhammadzoda was smuggled out of prison where he described the torture and ill-treatment he had suffered at the Vahdat police station following his detention. Independent journalist Zavqibek Saidamini was sentenced to seven years in prison after being convicted of alleged collaboration with banned organisations, including the Islamic Renaissance Party of Tajikistan (IRPT) and Group 24 on 4 November 2022. 
Both journalists had spoken out openly against the imprisonment of their colleagues Abdullo Gurbati and Daler Imomali in June 2022. According to relatives, Abdullo Ghurbati is expected to be released later in autumn 2026, while journalist Daler Emomali is expected to be released in 2027 following the application of the amnesty provisions.

Title: Arrest of protesters during Gen-Z protest anniversary
Content:
On 25 June 2026, at least 355 protesters were arrested during nationwide demonstrations marking the second anniversary of the 2024 Finance Bill protests. Nairobi recorded the highest number of arrests, with 161 people detained. The Cabinet Secretary for Interior stated that those arrested could face charges including robbery, vandalism, obstruction of roads and attempted theft.
The scale of the arrests raises concerns about the protection of freedom of peaceful assembly and the possible broad use of criminal charges against protesters. The Kenya National Commission on Human Rights called on the public to report cases of arrest or missing persons, reflecting wider concerns about the treatment and whereabouts of demonstrators.
Civil society organisations responded by activating support mechanisms, with the Law Society of Kenya and the Defenders Coalition establishing hotlines to assist those arrested, missing or otherwise affected by the demonstrations.
The scale of the arrests and the need for emergency support indicate the current restrictive enabling environment for civil society, particularly for groups supporting peaceful protest and accountability. This discourages participation, weakens trust in public institutions and increases the risks faced by civil society actors working to protect fundamental freedoms.

Title: Anti-LGBTIQ movement and discourses spread amid proposals to criminalize same-sex relations
Content:
While many civil society organizations are promoting inclusivity, human rights, and gender equality, a massive movement called “Anti Boti” has emerged in Indonesia. Initiated by the influencer @advokatmohammad in April 2026, the movement continues to generate a large following and targets individuals of diverse gender identities (LGBTQIA+). Comments made by followed include incitements to violence, such as “if you see a boti [derogatory term for gay person], beat them up on the spot”. The rise of this movement coincides with a proposal by the Indonesian Ulema Council (MUI) to criminalize same-sex relations and those ‘promoting’ LGBTQIA+. Prior to this, in October 2025, President Prabowo Subianto ratified Presidential Regulation (Perpres) Number 111 of 2025 concerning the General Policy on National Defense 2025–2029. Within the regulation, LGBTQIA+ is classified as a non-military threat to the state.
The classification through Perpres 111/2025 as well as the MUI’s proposal and the “anti boti” movement have led to an increase in anti-LGBTQIA+ discourses and harassment of LGBTQIA+ individuals and activists. Human rights organisations have already noted a surge in attacks against LGBTQIA+ activists, such as the harassment of students during Pride celebrations. Apart from individual human rights violations, these campaigns have affected social cohesion and created an environment of pervasive fear in public discourses. Civil society further assesses the movement and MUI’s proposal as carrying the potential to lead to the criminalization of same-sex relations, the imposition of punishment and sanctions on individuals based on their gender identify and sexual orientation, as well as to further violence.

Title: Civil society raises concerns regarding consultation process for proposed Non-Profit Organisations Act
Content:
On 10 July 2026, the Department of Co-operatives and Friendly Societies (DCFS), through the Charities Authority, hosted a sensitisation session entitled "Non-Profit Organisations Act: Building Stronger Foundations Through Registration and Compliance" to present broad proposals for the proposed Non-Profit Organisations Act, which are expected to be submitted to Cabinet for consideration. The session was attended by more than 250 representatives from charities, non-governmental organisations (NGOs), and other civil society organisations.
During the engagement, participants expressed concerns regarding the consultation process, noting that although proposals were presented through a PowerPoint presentation, the presentation and supporting written proposals would not be shared with stakeholders. Civil society organisations raised concerns that the absence of written proposals limits their ability to meaningfully analyse, consult internally, and provide informed feedback. Stakeholders questioned whether the consultation process is consistent with the Government of Jamaica's Code of Consultation Policy, which promotes meaningful stakeholder engagement in the development of legislation and public policy. The issue has prompted continued engagement among civil society organisations regarding the need for a more transparent and participatory legislative process.

Title: Halted Canadian resettlement and extradition risk for refugee Zhang Xin Yan
Content:
A UN-recognised Chinese refugee, detained by Thai authorities for an alleged illegal stay since May 2026, was prevented from departing for Canada despite having an approved resettlement agreement. On 8 July 2026, Zhang Xin Yan was intercepted at Suvarnabhumi Airport while preparing to board her flight. Although Canada had already approved her application, issued a visa, and secured her travel, Thai immigration officials forced her to cancel the flight and returned her to the Suan Phlu Immigration Detention Centre.
During a court hearing on 16 July 2026, a Thai Immigration Bureau representative testified that the resettlement was halted at the direct request of the Chinese Embassy in Bangkok. The Embassy sent a letter on 7 July 2026 demanding a delay, alleging her behaviour was damaging to China but providing no supporting evidence.
Because Zhang is wanted under Hong Kong's National Security Law for her involvement in the overseas-based "Hong Kong Parliament" in addition to other acts of dissent in China, she faces a high risk of arbitrary detention and an unfair trial should she be forced to return to China. As of now, Zhang remains at severe and imminent risk of refoulement.

Title: Intimidation of ‘Trip Journalist Team’ during Obi Island reporting: another blow to press freedom
Content:
On 17 July 2026, Project Multatuli posted on the platform X about an intimidation experienced by the ‘Journalist Trip Team,’ which consisted of Project Multatuli, Tempo, Konde, and Mongabay. This intimidation took the form of banning their activities on Obi Island, North Maluku, and the threat of physical assault. According to the post, the journalists intended to travel to Kawasi Village and Soligi Village to cover the social, environmental, and human rights impacts related to Harita Nickel’s industrial operations on Obi Island.
According to online sources, Harita Nickel’s operations on Obi Island are proceeding without a Free, Prior, and Informed Consent (FPIC) process, potentially damaging the environment and threatening endemic wildlife. Intimidation of journalists, including those covering environmental topics and the impact of extractive industries, has been happening repeatedly across Indonesia. Intimidation is often carried out by those in power, the government, oligarchs, and entities connected to public policy. Repeated acts of such intimidation create a systematic deterrence, making journalists hesitant to cover critical resource-extraction zones. Meanwhile, without national and global media coverage, rural populations impacted by industrial mining lose critical visibility and leverage in negotiating basic rights and environmental protections.
The Alliance of Independent Journalists (AJI) has condemned the harassment experienced by the ‘Journalist Trip Team’ as a form of intimidation that conflicts with the principles of press freedom. Furthermore, they are calling on several parties to take action, including: urging law enforcement officers to investigate the alleged intimidation and guarantee the safety of journalists and sources while reporting. Given the current state of democracy and human rights  in Indonesia, such practices are highly likely to persist in the future, if there is no protection for journalists and press freedom itself.

Title: Concerns over patterns of criminalization against civil society actors persist despite rulings highlighting irregularities in judicial proceedings
Content:
The Third Chamber of the Court of Appeals overturned the arrest warrants issued against 23 people linked to the case known as “Acuerdos Fraudulentos”, including former prosecutors from the Public Ministry, former Attorney General Thelma Aldana, and former head of the International Commission against Impunity in Guatemala (CICIG), Iván Velásquez. The ruling determined that those warrants exceeded the Chamber’s legal authority, in line with a criterion previously set by the Supreme Court of Justice.
The decision represents progress in terms of due process and legal oversight by correcting an action issued without the proper institutional authority. However, it does not bring an end to the criminal proceedings against the individuals concerned, several of whom are part of a group of former justice officials and actors linked to anti-corruption efforts who have faced judicial actions in recent years. In this context, civil society organizations and international bodies have expressed concern about the misuse of the justice system for political purposes against human rights defenders, former justice officials, and other critical actors, considering these cases part of a broader context of criminalization.
These concerns are also reflected in the criminal proceedings against peasant leader Leocadio Juracán, whose intermediate hearing was suspended and rescheduled for September 2026, prolonging his involvement in the case. For the organizations supporting him, this situation demonstrates the burden imposed by prolonged judicial processes, affecting both the individuals facing prosecution and their human rights defense and public oversight work.
The event has a direct impact on the enabling environment for civil society. While the ruling contributes to strengthening the rule of law and legal certainty, the continuation of lengthy judicial proceedings against actors involved in human rights defense, anti-corruption efforts, and community organizing raises concerns about the misuse of the justice system and its chilling effects on civic participation and the work of civil society organizations.

Title: Police harassment of peaceful individual commemorators on the “721 Incident” anniversary
Content:
On 21 July 2026, marking the anniversary of the Yuen Long mob attack (the "721 incident") in 2019, police deployed a pre-emptive presence to deter public commemoration. At Yuen Long Station at least 10 suspected plainclothes officers were stationed with multiple additional officers monitoring the underpass leading to the Light Rail station. This pre-emptive police deployment echoes previous observations on sensitive dates, such as 4 June, demonstrating a structural pattern where law enforcement proactively moves to prevent peaceful individual expression and assembly.
Despite this intimidating atmosphere, individuals courageously staged peaceful, solitary or two-person protests at the site to preserve historical memory. Officers routinely stopped and searched these peaceful commemorators, recorded their personal details, and physically obstructed their movement. While no formal arrests were made on site that day, this pre-emptive harassment serves to intimidate citizens and suppress public discourse.

Title: The National Libertarian Party Introduces a Bill That Would Require Organizations to Disclose Funds Received from Abroad
Content:

Title: Kast’s administration proposes using the Clave Única to access social media
Content:
On 11 June 2026, the Minister of Social Development and Family, María Jesús Wulf, announced during a panel discussion at the University of the Andes that the administration of President José Antonio Kast is considering a bill to require the use of the Clave Única as a means of accessing social media and digital platforms. The stated goal is to restrict minors’ access to these platforms by verifying their age without revealing their identity to technology companies.
The Clave Única, administered by Secretariat of Digital Government and used by more than 16 million Chileans to access nearly 1,700 public platforms, would act as an intermediary: it would inform the social media platform or the App Store whether the user meets the minimum age requirement. The initiative is part of a global trend toward regulating the digital world for children and adolescents, following in the footsteps of Australia, the United Kingdom, and Indonesia.
The announcement has sparked an intense debate, with some voices celebrating child protection and others warning of risks related to surveillance and the violation of fundamental rights.

Title: Announcements by the incoming government regarding the dismantling of institutions established under the Peace Agreement
Content:
During the week of 14 July 2026, President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella announced a series of measures aimed at significantly reducing the institutional framework created to implement the 2016 Final Peace Agreement. Among the announcements were the abolition of the Office of the High Commissioner for Peace, a reduction of approximately 90 per cent in the budget of the Special Jurisdiction for Peace (JEP), and the abolition or merger of bodies relating to reparations for victims, historical memory and the reintegration of former combatants. Furthermore, the new government announced the elimination of hundreds of posts associated with peace policy as part of an administrative austerity strategy.
The announcements prompted reactions from various stakeholders, such as former President Juan Manuel Santos, who warned that these decisions could affect the fulfilment of constitutional and international commitments undertaken by the Colombian State, although its institutional safeguards are quite robust and must be respected. The International Federation for Human Rights (FIDH), amongst other organisations, had expressed during the election period its concern about the possible weakening of the mechanisms created to guarantee victims’ rights and consolidate the implementation of the Agreement across the country.
Although the measures will still need to be translated into administrative, budgetary and legislative decisions before they can be implemented, the announcements represent a significant shift in the direction of public policy on peace and create a climate of uncertainty for civil society organisations involved in implementation, monitoring and advocacy.

Title: Ministry of Planning and Economic Development (MOPED) bans NGOs over regulatory compliance
Content:
The Ministry of Planning and Economic Development (MoPED) has revoked the registration certificates of 26 non-governmental organisations (NGOs) across Sierra Leone, citing persistent violations of the NGO Policy Framework and statutory requirements. In a press release dated 6 July 2026, they revoked the licenses of 7 NGOs, and an additional 19 NGOs in a press release dated 13 July 2026.
According to the Ministry, the decision follows a nationwide compliance verification exercise which revealed that the affected organisations failed to maintain identifiable office premises, report their development interventions, and meet mandatory legal and regulatory obligations necessary to retain their registration. MoPED said the revocation, which takes immediate effect, is part of efforts to strengthen accountability and transparency in the NGO sector while safeguarding public confidence. The Ministry stressed that compliant NGOs remain vital partners in Sierra Leone’s socio-economic development and reaffirmed its commitment to supporting organisations that adhere to the rules.
Civil Society Organizations including Campaign for Good Governance (CGG) welcome these strides to sanitize the NGO environment and safeguard public confidence, however, they remain concerned that these actions by MOPED to ban NGOs could be high-handedness to regulate the space using the NGO Policy Framework 2023, and this has affected mostly local NGOs. There are concerns that the policy does not prescribe for step-by-step punitive action against operational NGOs including warning and administrative review, instead of a straight ban. CGG is equally apprehensive that MOPED will use the policy as overreach to ban fully operational organizations who are critical of government under the guise of non compliance, and are encouraging MOPED to be fair and transparent with this process, to enhance public confidence.

Title: National Security Police raids on independent bookstores and supply-chain censorship
Content:
On 15 July 2026, coinciding with the opening day of the Hong Kong Book Fair, the police National Security Department raided two independent bookstores in Hong Kong —Have A Nice Stay (留下書舍) and Greenfield Book Store (田園書屋). Five individuals were arrested under Article 24 of the Safeguarding National Security Ordinance for allegedly displaying and selling publications with "seditious intent". The police operation was reportedly triggered by a referral from the Customs and Excise Department, which intercepted an overseas shipment containing books such as Acropolis Publications' Let Only Red Flowers Bloom: Identity and Belonging in Xi Jinping's China (Chinese version) as well as memoirs and works by former lawmakers Emily Lau and Shiu Ka-chun (Prisoner Outside Prison).
This enforcement action triggered immediate, systemic self-censorship across the international logistics sector. The Taiwan branch of Hong Kong logistics firm Jaguar Logistics (嘉達國際物流) claimed that because entire containers were previously detained by Hong Kong Customs at significant financial loss, it updated its operating rules to require clients to submit book lists in advance to verify compliance with National Security laws, and outright refused to deliver goods to four independent bookstores searched by police. Meanwhile, Secretary for Security Chris Tang reiterated that the government will not publish a list of banned books, placing full legal risk on booksellers by comparing it to "food sellers having a responsibility to avoid poisoning customers." The public arrest of bookstore staff sparked international solidarity, including actions in Taipei where supporters wore t-shirts reading "I am a bookstore staff member."

Title: New Gabonese debates on the possibility of being a civil society leader and an elected representative of a political party at the same time
Content:
On 15 July 2026, the second Vice-President of the Economic, Social, Environmental and Cultural Council (CESEC), sitting on behalf of civil society, Geoffroy Foumboula Libeka Makosso, was invited by the coalition of civil society organisations to chair a conference on this subject; the theme of the conference was “ Gabonese Civil Society: between pluralist democracy and participatory democracy ”. During this conference, the issue of holding dual roles as ‘an elected representative of a political party and a civil society leader’ was raised by a section of Gabonese civil society.
Within this context, two contrasting perspectives have been raised. The first is the view that a member of civil society should not belong to a political party for ethical reasons, given that civil society must be independent and therefore politically neutral. This view is also supported by the former leader of civil society and president of the political party, the National Party for Labour and Progress (PNTP), Jean Rémy Yama, who believes that, for ethical reasons, a political leader should not hold positions of responsibility within civil society.
The counter-argument is the idea that a civil society leader has the right to join a political party and hold influential positions within it, whilst retaining the same powers within civil society; preventing them from doing so would constitute a restriction on the exercise of their rights. This argument is put forward by one of the senior officials of the president’s political party, the Union Démocratiques des Bâtisseurs (UDB), Georges Mpaga, Fifth Secretary of the Senate Bureau and a leader who remains active within civil society.

Title: The Constitutional Court upholds the mural ‘Las cuchas tienen razón’ and strengthens safeguards for freedom of expression and historical memory
Content:
The Constitutional Court issued a ruling recognising that the mural “Las cuchas tienen razón” constitutes an expression protected by the Constitution, as it is closely linked to the rights to freedom of expression, freedom of artistic creation, historical memory and the right to the truth for the victims of the armed conflict. The decision responds to several applications for constitutional protection filed following the censorship and vandalism of the mural in various cities across the country.
The High Court rejected the request to remove the mural submitted by a member of the public and, instead, upheld the fundamental rights invoked by human rights and historical memory organisations. It also ordered Councillor Andrés Felipe Rodríguez (Gury), who had encouraged and publicised acts of vandalism against the artwork, to issue a public apology and acknowledge the legitimacy of artistic expression. The Court also urged the local authorities to take measures to prevent further acts of censorship and to promote awareness-raising campaigns on historical memory.
With this decision, the Court sets an important precedent regarding the constitutional protection of artistic expression and remembrance initiatives promoted by social organisations and victims’ groups, reaffirming that political disagreement cannot justify arbitrary restrictions on freedom of expression.

Title: The Court of Algiers has upheld Fethi Ghares’s two-year prison sentence
Content:
On 21 July 2026, the Criminal Division of the Court of Algiers upheld in full the judgement handed down on 21 October 2025 by the Hussein Dey Magistrates’ Court against Fethi Ghares, national coordinator of the Democratic and Social Movement (MDS), a political party which is itself subject to a judicial suspension. The sentence handed down is two years’ imprisonment, together with a fine of 300,000 dinars and the confiscation of the seized items.
Fethi Ghares was prosecuted under Articles 146 and 196 bis of the Penal Code, for ‘contempt of a public authority’ and ‘spreading false information’ respectively, both of which are deemed capable of undermining public order and public security. The charges are based primarily on public political statements and posts on social media. The defence had sought his acquittal, arguing that the acts constituted the peaceful exercise of freedom of political expression, whilst the prosecution had sought a harsher sentence. This confirmation on appeal reinforces concerns regarding the criminalisation of political criticism, pluralism and the independence of the judiciary.

Title: Bill Eliminating Inclusive Language in Public Services Passes
Content:
On Wednesday, 17 June 2026, the Chilean Chamber of Deputies approved a draft resolution calling on President José Antonio Kast to eliminate the use of inclusive language in all of the country’s public services. The initiative, spearheaded by the UDI caucus and other right-wing lawmakers, was backed by 85 votes in favor, 53 against, and one abstention.
The text instructs the Executive Branch to “revoke circulars, resolutions, or other administrative acts that mandate the use of inclusive language in various public services and to issue a decree mandating the correct use of the Spanish language, prohibiting any grammatical distortion based on gender, ethnicity, or other identity-based classifications.” Congressman Jorge Alessandri (UDI), president of the Chamber, read the proposal, noting that it seeks to “immediately prohibit any grammatical distortion based on gender, ethnicity, or other identity-based classifications.” Republican Congressman Cristián Araya celebrated the measure on social media with a “Goodbye to the ‘woke’ dictatorship!”

Title: Kast Proposes Creating a National Registry of Acts of Vandalism and Incivility
Content:
On 15 June, the government of José Antonio Kast submitted to the Chamber of Deputies a bill establishing the National Registry of Acts of Vandalism and Incivility. The initiative, one of the flagship measures announced in the State of the Union address on June 1, establishes a public, electronic, and national registry—administered by the Civil Registry—in which individuals with final convictions for 33 criminal offenses will be registered.
These are divided into “acts of vandalism” (crimes such as assaulting law enforcement, threats, murder of prosecutors, hijacking public transportation, or small-scale drug trafficking) and “incivilities” (administrative offenses such as drug use in public, unauthorized graffiti, or the illegal sale of alcohol).
Those included in the registry will face penalties ranging from the loss of social benefits—such as free higher education, the Universal Guaranteed Pension (PGU), and housing subsidies—to the inability to renew a driver’s license, obtain a passport, or attend professional sporting events.
The bill was introduced as a matter of utmost urgency and is already facing criticism from the opposition, which has filed a constitutional objection and warned about its classist nature and potential unconstitutionality, as well as the risk that it could be used to persecute student and social protests.

Title: The New National Security Plan May Have Negative Implications for the Enabling Environment
Content:
On 14 July 2026, through Executive Decree No. 448, President Daniel Noboa brought into force the National Comprehensive Security Plan 2025–2029. The document introduces several strategies that could have negative implications for the enabling environment for civil society. These include strengthening security operations against "violent extremism" (Strategy 2.1), a concept that is ambiguously defined in the plan; using traditional and digital media to reinforce positive public perceptions of security (Strategy 2.5); increasing monitoring, auditing, and oversight activities targeting national and international NGOs, foundations, and corporations (Strategy 4.6); and re-establishing specialized military courts (Strategy 4.7), which were abolished in Ecuador in 2008.
Overall, these strategies pose potential risks to the freedoms of association, expression, and peaceful assembly, as well as to the editorial independence of the media. The broad and vague definition of "violent extremism" could facilitate its application against organizations and social movements, potentially criminalizing social mobilization. Meanwhile, Strategy 4.6 reinforces the Noboa administration's apparent intention to treat all civil society organizations as potential vehicles for money laundering and the financing of criminal actors. Furthermore, the use of the media to "strengthen" positive perceptions of security could increase government influence over media narratives, affecting the objective reporting of violence, crime, and the conduct of members of the security forces. Finally, the proposal to create specialized military courts could limit the ability of activists and civil society organizations to scrutinize future cases of human rights violations committed by members of the Armed Forces during security operations.
To date, no public statements have been issued by civil society organizations regarding the potential impact of these security strategies on the enabling environment.

Title: Controversial Cybercrime & Computer Misuse Act 2026 in effect
Content:
On 17 July 2026, the government of South Sudan officially began enforcing the Cybercrime and Computer Misuse Act, 2026, following Presidential Directive No. 03/2026. The law establishes a National Cyber-Security Steering Committee that will be chaired by the Minister of Justice, and a National Cyber-Security Task Force to be led by the Internal Security Bureau of the National Security Service.
The Act criminalizes a wide range of online activities where Section 42 targets content deemed to promote tribalism, incite violence, or threaten national security, while Section 44 prohibits “false or misleading information” that could damage reputations, undermine public confidence, or cause panic. Offences such as cyberbullying and harassment carry penalties of up to five years imprisonment.
Government officials argue the law is necessary to protect digital infrastructure and ensure stability ahead of the December 2026 elections. However, civil society organizations and media groups have raised concerns that the Act’s broad and vague provisions could be used to suppress freedom of expression, silence journalists, and restrict civic activism online.

Title: Court rules against the National Police over the death of Dilan Cruz and reaffirms the right to prote
Content:
The Administrative Court of Cundinamarca handed down a second-instance ruling, on 25 June 2026and made public on 10 July 2026. Best regards!holding the National Police responsible for the death of Dilan Cruz, which occurred during the demonstrations that took place as part of the national strike in November 2019. The ruling concludes that the use of ammunition classified as ‘less lethal’ was disproportionate and unjustified, and that the police’s actions violated the young protester’s fundamental rights.
The judgement increases the compensation awarded to the family, orders the National Police to hold a public ceremony acknowledging their responsibility and offering an apology, and emphasises that the exercise of the constitutional right to protest must not put the lives of those participating peacefully at risk. Furthermore, the Court rejected the arguments that Dilan Cruz’s behaviour justified the use of force, noting that throwing back tear gas does not constitute a threat that would justify the use of a potentially lethal weapon.
The ruling also questions the institutional classification of this type of weapon as ‘less lethal’, noting that this designation may have led to an erroneous assessment of the risks associated with its use. Although the decision settles the State’s financial liability, proceedings to establish the individual liability of the officers involved are still ongoing.

Title: Political violence ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections
Content:
Ahead of the 2026 Local Government Elections, scheduled for 6 November 2026, concerns over political violence intensified following a series of attacks and killings involving local political figures and election candidates.
On 20 June 2026, Sinovuyo Dyokwe, a Democratic Alliance (DA) ward by-election candidate and community activist in Du Noon, Cape Town was shot and killed while returning home after participating in the first day of the Independent Electoral Commission (IEC) voter registration weekend. Reports subsequently emerged that Dyokwe had allegedly received extortion threats before her death, prompting investigators to examine whether organised crime, rather than party-political rivalry may have been a contributing factor. At the time of reporting, no arrests had been made.
Later that day, Sicelo Mleve, the African National Congress (ANC) Ward 27 councillor in the Nelson Mandela Bay Metropolitan Municipality and a member of the ANC's Nelson Mandela Regional Executive Committee, was shot and killed by unknown gunmen while holding a meeting in his office in Zwide, Gqeberha, Eastern Cape. At approximately 18:50 PM two-armed men entered the office during a meeting of about 10 people, demanding cellphones and allegedly asking for him by name before shooting him. The other attendees escaped unharmed. According to reports, Mleve had previously received threats and had previously been provided with protection, which he had reportedly relinquished before the attack Two suspects, aged 20 and 21 were later arrested and appeared in Brighton Magistrate’s Court on 3 July 2026 in connection with the murder.
The killings prompted widespread condemnation and renewed concerns over violence targeting political figures ahead of the elections. The DA described Dyokwe's murder as an attack on democratic participation and called for a thorough investigation. The South African Communist Party (SACP) similarly condemned Mleve's killing, warning that it reflected an escalation of political violence and organised criminal activity in the Eastern Cape. These attacks underscored the persistent risks faced by local political representatives and candidates during election periods and highlighted the need for effective investigations, enhanced security measures and stronger protections to safeguard democratic participation and electoral integrity.
Enabling principles: 1. Respect and protection of fundamental freedoms
Respect and protection: Freedom of expression

Title: South Africa: Nationwide Anti-Migrant Protests Trigger Violence, Displacement and Rights Concerns
Content:
The nationwide anti-migrant protests held on 30 June 2026 were organised by a coalition of more than 20 organisations, including the March and March Movement. The coalition submitted memoranda to government officials across several provinces outlining their demands, which included stricter enforcement of immigration laws, tighter border controls, increased funding for the Border Management Authority (BMA) and the Department of Home Affairs (DHA), as well as measures to reserve township economic opportunities for South African citizens.
The South African Police Service (SAPS) reported that 120 protests took place across several provinces including Gauteng, KwaZulu-Natal, Mpumalanga, Limpopo and the Western Cape. Of these, 108 protests remained peaceful, while 12 required police intervention after violence broke out in several communities. The unrest resulted in looting, attacks on foreign-owned businesses, clashes with law enforcement, and the displacement of thousands of migrants who fled their homes in anticipation of, or in response to, the protests. More than 900 people were arrested during and immediately after the protests for offences, including public violence, looting, robbery, immigration-related violations and harbouring of undocumented migrants
The unrest resulted in at least one confirmed fatality. A man was shot dead during the looting of foreign-owned informal corner shops.
March and March leader Jocinta Ngobese-Zuma stated that protests would continue every Thursday until the government implements stricter border controls and intensify efforts to remove undocumented migrants from the country.
In response to the violence and heightened tensions, many foreign nationals fled their communities to seek safety. Approximately 25,000 migrants from other African countries were reportedly repatriated.
The South African government condemned the violence and reiterated that immigration enforcement is the responsibility of the state and not private individuals or anti-migrant groups. President Cyril Ramaphosa acknowledged public concerns regarding undocumented migrants but warned against vigilantism, xenophobia and attacks on foreign nationals. Human rights organisations, including Amnesty International South Africa criticised the protests for scapegoating migrants. They argued that the underlying challenges are rooted in the legacy of apartheid, persistent inequality, and shortcomings in the country's asylum system.

Title: Workers’ trade union dissolution and reinstatement
Content:
On 8 July 2026, the Bank of South Sudan Governor issued an administrative order dissolving the workers’ trade union, citing an “illegal general assembly.” This was after the staffs of the bank organized a sit-in strike for salary arrears that had accumulated for more than 24 months. The staff however intensified their strike action in protest. The union leadership rejected the dissolution as unconstitutional, arguing that only the General Assembly could dissolve the body, not management.
The wider civil society made a call to the bank's leadership to consider revoking the dissolution as it was determined unprocedural and inconsistent with the legal instrument that guides the regulation of the union, such as the Workers’ Trade Union Act, 2013. Furthermore, the order contradicted South Sudan's Transitional Constitution that allows freedoms of assembly and association under article 25. The bank's governor was compelled to reinstate the union after sustained pressure 24 hours after its dissolution. Both the bank leadership and the workers union announced an ongoing peaceful and constructive negotiations. The union suspended the strike.
