Title: Alleged gendered online targeting of activist by a government minister
Content:
In the first week of July 2026, Senator and Minister in the Ministry of Housing Phillip Edward Alexander published a Facebook post about social media activist Suzette Louwe. The post, which was later deleted, contained personal allegations relating to alleged intimate photographs, Louwe’s employment and marriage, and the conception of her children. Alexander denied that his comments were derogatory or constituted an attack on women, said he had not claimed to possess intimate images, and framed the post as a response to Louwe’s criticism of public figures.
The incident prompted widespread online criticism and competing petitions. By 10 July, Louwe’s petition calling for Alexander to be held accountable reportedly had more than 800 signatures, while Alexander’s counter-petition had nearly 300. In Louwe’s formal petition to the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights (IACHR), she states that she complained to the Prime Minister on 11 July and alleges cyber-harassment, gender-based defamation, violations of privacy, and intimidation. The petition document does not show an IACHR acknowledgment or registration number, so submission and acceptance should be treated separately.
The event negatively affects the enabling environment for civil society because the reported use of a senior public official’s platform to make personal, sexualised and family-related allegations against an activist may create fear of reprisals among people who criticise the government. It may particularly discourage women activists from participating in public debate or engaging in advocacy online. The incident also weakens supportive public discourse around civil society, undermines trust between civic actors and the state, and raises concerns about whether activists can operate safely in digital spaces without reputational or privacy-related attacks. The absence of a timely and transparent institutional response may further contribute to perceptions that public officials can target civil society actors without effective accountability.
Enabling principles: 1. Respect and protection of fundamental freedoms | 5. Supportive public culture and discourses on civil society | 6. Access to a secure digital environment
Respect and protection: Freedom of expression

Title: State fails to substantively address civil society warnings over emergency detentions
Content:
On 18–19 July 2026, local media reported renewed concerns from human rights defenders about the use of Preventive Detention Orders (PDOs) during Trinidad and Tobago’s continuing State of Emergency. Former Trinidad and Tobago Human Rights Commission head Denise Pitcher, veteran human rights defender Diana Mahabir-Wyatt, and constitutional lawyer Subhas Panday raised concerns about prolonged detention without charge, inadequate medical care, detention conditions, limited access to legal representation, weak independent oversight, and the effectiveness of the State of Emergency Review Tribunal. Approximately 434 PDO notices have reportedly been issued, but no complete public record has been made available showing how many detainees have been charged, released, convicted, or remain in detention. These concerns follow a statement by the Inter-American Commission on Human Rights calling for stronger judicial oversight, transparency, accountability, due process protections, and safeguards against arbitrary detention.
The event negatively affects the enabling environment for civil society organisations, particularly State openness and responsiveness and the protection of fundamental freedoms. Although human rights defenders and CSOs remain able to speak publicly, the absence of a substantive State response and accessible detention data limits their ability to monitor emergency powers, assess their proportionality, advocate for affected persons, and hold public authorities accountable. Continued non-responsiveness may weaken meaningful civil society participation in national security decision-making and reduce confidence that human rights advocacy will influence government policy or corrective action.

Title: New AML/CFT Laws raise concerns for the regulatory environment for civil society
Content:
On 9 July 2026, the Sri Lankan Parliament passed three amendments to the country’s anti-money laundering and counter-terrorist financing framework. These laws are  the Prevention of Money Laundering Bill that was passed in line with the Supreme Court’s determination, and the Financial Transactions Reporting (Amendment) Bill with amendments, although the exact changes have not yet been made public. In addition, the Convention on the Suppression of Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill was passed without amendments. However, these Bills will only come into effect once they receive the Speaker's endorsement, and the date of endorsement has not yet been confirmed.
The Bills were introduced through a fast-tracked process in April and May 2026 ahead of Sri Lanka’s Financial Action Task Force (FATF) mutual evaluation, with significantly limited opportunities for public consultation and civil society engagement.
Their passage therefore raises concerns for Sri Lanka’s enabling environment for civil society. The Convention on the Suppression of Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill significantly expands surveillance and interception powers for law enforcement, including monitoring of non-profit organisations deemed “high risk,” such as those engaged in human rights advocacy, without clearly defined or objective criteria. This raises concerns about increased scrutiny of civil society activity even in the absence of financial crime risk. The Financial Transactions Reporting (Amendment) Bill grants extensive and potentially vague powers to the Financial Intelligence Unit (FIU), with limited safeguards against arbitrary application.
Civil society actors have previously  challenged all three Bills before the Supreme Court, arguing that several provisions risk undermining freedom of association, expression, equality before the law and access to judicial remedies. Although the Court upheld the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Bill and the Convention on the Suppression of Terrorist Financing (Amendment) Bill as constitutional, and only Clause 22 and Clause 39 in the Financial Transactions Reporting (Amendment) Bill as unconstitutional. While the Supreme Court identified only limited inconsistencies with the Constitution, stakeholders argue that the breadth of discretionary authority could still result in disproportionate regulatory burdens on civil society organisations and related professionals. Similarly, the Prevention of Money Laundering (Amendment) Bill removes the requirement for a prior conviction in establishing predicate offences, potentially lowering the threshold for enforcement actions. Civil society actors caution that this could enable the misuse of AML/CFT frameworks to constrain legitimate civic, advocacy, and economic activities.
Overall, the reforms reflect a broader pattern of expanding executive authority through financial and security legislation, contributing to heightened regulatory scrutiny and concerns over the gradual narrowing of civic space in Sri Lanka. The passage of the Bills marks a significant step in this legislative process, with their practical impact depending on the final text of the amendments and their implementation following the Speaker's endorsement.

Title: Civil society organisations raise concerns regarding proposed Non-Profit Organisations Act and its potential impact on the operation of charities and NGOs
Content:
Representatives of several Jamaican civil society organisations and charitable foundations have publicly expressed concerns regarding the Government's proposed Non-Profit Organisations (NPO) Act, which is expected to replace the existing legislative framework governing charities by October 2026.  During a Jamaica Observer Monday Exchange, on the 28 June 2026, representatives of the Council of Voluntary Social Services (CVSS), EVE for Life, the Phillip and Christine Gore Family Foundation, and Deaf Can Coffee stated that, while they support transparency and accountability within the sector, the proposed legislation could impose additional regulatory and administrative burdens that may adversely affect the operation of non-profit organisations, particularly smaller volunteer-run entities.
Stakeholders also expressed concern that organisations expected to be regulated under the proposed legislation have not been meaningfully consulted during its development. They cautioned that increased compliance obligations may divert already limited resources away from service delivery, advocacy, and community development initiatives, potentially affecting vulnerable groups that rely on support provided by civil society organisations. The issue raises broader questions regarding stakeholder participation in legislative reform, the operational environment for civil society, and the balance between regulatory oversight and the effective functioning of non-profit organisations.

Title: Fine imposed on news website sparks press freedom concerns
Content:
In June 2026, a public controversy emerged in Mongolia after the news website Zuv.mn was reportedly fined 20 million MNT following a complaint by an official of a state-owned company over the use of his photograph in public-interest reporting in January 2026. Media reports indicated that the photograph had been treated as “biometric information” under personal data protection rules, raising concerns about the application of privacy protections in a journalistic context.
The decision prompted strong reactions from journalists, media organisations and civil society actors. The Mongolian Journalists Association submitted demands to the Speaker of Parliament, the Prime Minister and the National Human Rights Commission, warning that the sanction could undermine press freedom and the public’s right to information. Zuv.mn also publicly challenged the decision and requested clarification from the National Human Rights Commission on the legal basis for the sanction.
The case also drew political criticism. Prime Minister Nyam-Osor Uchral argued that the use of a public official’s photograph in journalistic reporting should not be treated as unlawful use of biometric data, describing the sanction as an infringement on freedom of expression and the public’s right to know. The Speaker of Parliament similarly criticised the decision and called for accountability for officials involved in restricting press freedom.
The case highlights growing concern over the balance between personal data protection and media freedom in Mongolia. While privacy protections are important, applying them in a way that penalises reporting on public officials and matters of public interest may create a chilling effect on investigative journalism and weaken public oversight.

Title: Court acquits protesters and orders investigation into possible false complaint
Content:
On 27 June 2026, the Criminal Court of the First Judicial Circuit of San José acquitted three protesters accused of aggravated resistance in connection with a demonstration against police brutality held outside the Legislative Assembly on 9 September 2023. Ana Carolina Marín Durán, Mar Fournier Pereira and Valeri Salas Solís had been accused of assaulting a police officer during the protest.
The court found that the audiovisual and photographic evidence did not corroborate the allegations and identified serious shortcomings in the process used to identify the defendants. The Public Prosecutor’s Office also requested their acquittal after concluding that the alleged conduct could not be proven.
It is worth noting that the judge ordered that the evidence be forwarded to the competent authorities to investigate whether a potentially false or malicious complaint had been lodged against two of the protesters. This goes beyond the acquittal itself, as it raises the possibility of holding those responsible to account for the misuse of criminal proceedings against people exercising their right to protest.
The judgement therefore constitutes a positive example of judicial oversight in defence of due process and civil liberties. It reaffirms that charges arising from demonstrations must be supported by credible evidence and properly verified before criminal proceedings are initiated. The investigation ordered could also help to deter unfounded accusations that might intimidate demonstrators and discourage further public participation.

Title: Progress in the formation of the Nomination Commission for the selection of the Comptroller General of Accounts
Content:
The formation of the Nomination Commission for the selection of the Comptroller General of Accounts (CGC) made significant progress with the unanimous election of Miquel Cortés, Rector of Rafael Landívar University (URL), as the Commission’s president. The decision was adopted by the Forum of Rectors, with the participation of thirteen universities, and marks the beginning of the Commission’s organizational phase, during which it will evaluate applicants and prepare the shortlist of six candidates to be submitted to Congress for the election of the next Comptroller General of Accounts.
The selection of this authority is a significant process for democratic institutions, given the role of the Comptroller General of Accounts in overseeing the use of public resources and strengthening accountability mechanisms. The session was held publicly, allowing observers and media outlets to attend, which represents a positive element for transparency and openness throughout the process. Civil society organizations specialized in institutional monitoring, such as Movimiento Pro Justicia and Guatemala Visible, welcomed the appointment of the Commission’s president, while noting that the Commission’s legitimacy will depend on the independence, impartiality, and performance of all its members.
The process will continue with the incorporation of representatives from professional associations, the call for applicants, and the review of their qualifications, which are key stages in completing the Commission’s composition. Although this step represents a positive signal for institutional transparency, continued monitoring will be needed regarding the legal actions associated with the process and the absence of the University of San Carlos of Guatemala (USAC), as these factors may affect the Commission’s legitimacy and the enabling environment for civil society, particularly in terms of civic participation, access to information, and independent oversight.

Title: Launch of FCRA 2.0 portal amidst talks of new FCRA bill
Content:
On 30 June 2026, Union Home Minister Amit Shah launched the FCRA 2.0 Portal in New Delhi, fully digitising all services under the Foreign Contribution (Regulation) Act, 2010 — including fresh registrations, renewals, annual returns, and compliance applications. Hosted on MeghRaj, the National Government Cloud, the portal integrates Aadhaar-based authentication, e-Sign facility, Optical Character Recognition (OCR)-based document verification, and Application Programming Interface (API) linkages with Permanent Account Numbers (PAN), NGO Darpan, and the Institute of Chartereed Accountatns” (ICAI) Unique Document Identification Number (UDIN) system. The 2026 FCRA Amendment Rules are built directly into the portal’s workflow. The government framed the launch as a step toward “Minimum Government, Maximum Governance,” aimed at simplifying compliance for genuine organisations while strengthening real-time monitoring of foreign contributions. Future features including an AI chatbot, FCRA mobile app, and dedicated bank dashboard are planned but not yet live.
The FCRA 2.0 launch follows a decade-long trajectory of regulatory tightening around foreign funding for civil society in India. The FCRA Amendment Rules, 2026, notified on 22 June 2026 — just days before this portal launch — introduced twelve new conditions including purpose-based and geography-specific registration, a minimum utilisation threshold for renewal, and restrictions on foreign nationals in leadership positions. The FCRA 2.0 portal was launched to operationalise these new rules digitally.
By embedding the 2026 Rules directly into the portal’s workflow, the government has made the restrictive provisions — purpose-based registration, geography-specific licences, instalment-release conditions, and leadership restrictions — operationally inescapable. This represents a qualitative shift from a regulatory framework that could be challenged or interpreted flexibly, to one that is enforced automatically through digital architecture. While thousands of active FCRA-registered organisations are directly affected, the organisations most acutely affected are small and medium-sized CSOs working in remote or conflict-sensitive areas, organisations with international governance structures or foreign board members, and those engaged in rights-based advocacy, humanitarian work, or cross-border programming.
At the same time, requirements are expected to be further restricted in the coming months. The government has signalled that a new FCRA Act is anticipated in the upcoming monsoon session of Parliament. This Act is intended to fully replace the previous FCRA Act and his would represent the most significant restructuring of India’s foreign funding regulatory environment in over a decade, with long-term consequences for the scale, independence, and diversity of India’s civil society sector.

Title: Arbitrary arrest of journalist Mohamed Jama raises concerns over press freedom in Puntland
Content:
On 14 July 2026, journalist Mohamed Jama was arrested by officers of the Puntland Intelligence Service (PISA) in Bosaso, Puntland. According to the National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ), he was taken to a PISA detention facility without any publicly disclosed legal basis for his arrest. Media freedom organizations reported that authorities declined to provide information regarding his detention, raising concerns over due process and transparency. The arrest occurred shortly after his reporting on business closures and protests over increased import taxes in Bosaso.
The National Union of Somali Journalists (NUSOJ), the Somali Journalists Syndicate (SJS), and the International Federation of Journalists (IFJ) condemned the arrest, stating that it reflects a pattern of increasing pressure on independent journalists in Puntland. They called for his immediate release and urged authorities to respect press freedom and Somalia's obligations under national and international human rights standards. The incident raises concerns about the safety of journalists and the ability of the media to report freely on issues of public interest.

Title: The Central Board of Direct Taxes condones delay in filing Form 10AB for Section 80G approval
Content:
On 2 July 2026, India’s Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) issued Circular No. 06/2026, grantingcondonation of delay for charitable and religious trusts that submitted Form 10AB for the renewal of Section 80G(5) approval after the 30 September 2025 deadline. The measure applies to applications filed electronically between 1 October 2025 and 31 March 2026, including cases previously rejected solely due to late submission.
The measure follows representations from organisations whose 80G approvals were due to expire on 31 March 2026 and who were unable to meet the deadline due to genuine hardship during the transition to the new Registered Non-Profit Organisation (RNPO) framework introduced under the Income Tax Act, 2025. Under this framework, most charitable registrations are now valid for five years and require periodic renewal through Form 10AB, replacing the earlier largely perpetual approval system.
The Central Board of Direct Taxes (CBDT) clarified that delays will be condoned, but applications will continue to be assessed on their merits by the relevant tax authorities, with decisions expected by 31 December 2026.
The circular represents a positive but limited development for the enabling environment by providing corrective relief to organisations affected by the transition and protecting access to a key domestic funding mechanism. Maintaining 80G eligibility allows donors to continue claiming tax deductions on contributions, which is particularly important for smaller and grassroots organisations with limited compliance capacity. However, the measure does not remove the broader compliance challenges introduced by the new renewal regime. The case highlights the need for continued monitoring of how administrative requirements affect the sustainability and funding stability of civil society organisations in India.

Title: Travel ban imposed on journalist Mustapha Benfodil without prior notic
Content:
On 13 July 2026, the journalist, writer and playwright Mustapha Benfodil was turned back by the border police whilst attempting to travel to the Avignon Festival. It was on this occasion that he discovered he was subject to a ban on leaving the country — ISTN — without having been notified of any judicial or administrative decision beforehand. The editorial team of the magazine NAQD links this measure to his summons by the police on 18 January 2026, following the publication in El Watan of a review of the magazine’s issue 44 on shale gas. During an interrogation lasting approximately three hours, he was reportedly threatened and told verbally that an ISTN might be imposed on him.
In an open letter, NAQD condemned an arbitrary restriction on freedom of movement and an obstruction of journalistic work. The case, which has also been reported by Le Matin d’Algérie and La Radio des Sans Voix, has a negative impact on the environment conducive to civil society. It reinforces self-censorship, limits journalists’ participation in international exchanges and creates legal uncertainty surrounding restrictive measures that have not been notified.

Title: Deregistration of opposition parties limits political pluralism and threatens freedom of association
Content:
On 14 June 2026, Justice Peter Lifu of the Federal High Court in Abuja ordered the deregistration of the African Democratic Congress (ADC) and four other political parties over alleged constitutional breaches, prompting the ADC to reject the ruling as judicial rascality and a plot to cripple opposition ahead of the 2027 elections. The stated ground for the deregistration were that the parties allegedly failed the constitutional threshold of electoral support for continued registration, especially under Section 225A/225 of the Constitution and related electoral rules. The Court of Appeal, presided over by Justices Mohammed A. Danjuma, Adebunkunola A. Banjoko, and Oyejoju O. Oyewumi, had previously issued a stay of execution on 22 May 2026, ordering Justice Lifu to halt further action in the deregistration process pending the appeal hearing scheduled for 27 October 2026, in Appeal CA/ABJ/CV/569/2026 and suit No. FHC/ABJ/CS/2637/2025. Despite this, the Federal High Court proceeded with the deregistration issued on 14 June 2026. On 16 June 2026, the Court of Appeal issued another stay of execution halting enforcement of Justice Lifu’s deregistration order.
Critics, including former Vice President Senator David Mark and the Conference of Nigeria Political Parties, have condemned the deregistration as part of President Tinubu’s alleged bid to undermine opposition and entrench a one-party state, raising concerns about threats to Nigeria’s democracy. The deregistration is considered a case of improper judicial or administrative interference, highlighting risks to freedom of association. Political participation and political pluralism are further undermined with the deregistration threat directly affecting opposition competition and voter choice. The fact that the deregistration proceeded despite a Court of Appeal stay of execution decision also weakens institutional credibility and the rule of law.

Title: Proposed AI data centres raise transparency, consultation and digital-governance concerns
Content:
On 10 July 2026, the Government of Trinidad and Tobago announced three memoranda of understanding with United States companies, including two proposals for large-scale artificial-intelligence data centres. Ernst & Young LLP is associated with a proposed 300-megawatt facility, while Hummingbird AI Holdings LLC proposed a 150-megawatt facility that could eventually expand to 500 megawatts. The Government stated that the MoUs establish a framework for collaboration and due diligence rather than final development approval, and that technical, environmental and regulatory assessments would be completed before construction.
Government officials subsequently identified the Debe Special Economic Zone as the intended location and said that purpose-built ponds and, later, desalination facilities would prevent the projects from affecting residential and commercial water supplies. Debe residents, environmental advocates and technical experts nevertheless raised concerns about the absence of prior public consultation and publicly available information on water, electricity, land use, environmental effects, project costs, data protection and cybersecurity.
On 12 July, conservation researcher Syam Nath launched a Change.org petition asking the Government to suspend approvals until independent environmental, water-resource and infrastructure assessments are published and subjected to public consultation. When checked on 13 July 2026, the petition displayed 11,459 verified signatures; this number is changing rapidly. The situation also has implications for the enabling environment for civil society, as the lack of early transparency and structured consultation limits CSOs’ ability to access information, participate meaningfully in decision-making processes and hold authorities accountable.

Title: The Supreme Electoral Tribunal presents the calendar for the 2027 General Elections
Content:
The Supreme Electoral Tribunal (TSE) of Guatemala presented the schedule with the main planned dates for the 2027 General Elections during a meeting with representatives of the active political parties. The plan establishes that the official call for elections will take place on 22 January, 2027. The registration of candidates will run from 23 January to 20 March. The electoral campaign will take place from 29 March to 25 June. The first round will be held on 27 June, 2027. If a second presidential round is necessary, it would be held on 22 August.
The early presentation of the calendar constitutes a positive step in institutional planning and contributes to generating greater certainty about the stages of the upcoming electoral process. Likewise, the TSE reported that it has already begun the evaluation and recruitment of citizens to integrate the electoral boards, temporary bodies responsible for organizing and overseeing the elections.
The announcement comes in a pre-electoral context characterized by broad participation of political parties and possible candidacies for 2027. While the existence of numerous political organizations expands electoral competition, challenges persist related to the programmatic differentiation of some parties, the quality of the political offer, and the conditions of transparency and equality during the process.
The presentation of this electoral calendar facilitates citizen observation and monitoring by civil society organizations. It also creates opportunities to promote informed voting and to monitor key aspects such as political financing, the participation of women, indigenous peoples, and youth, as well as respect for the freedoms of expression, association, and participation. In the coming months, continued monitoring is needed to assess whether the implementation of the electoral calendar indeed translates into a transparent, participatory process with equitable conditions that strengthen public trust and democratic quality.

Title: Law Association challenges no-protest zones and continued State of Emergency
Content:
On 25 June 2026, the Law Association of Trinidad and Tobago (LATT), a civil-society professional association, publicly challenged the scope and justification of Emergency Powers restrictions that prohibit public protests and demonstrations within 500 metres of 15 designated locations. The State of Emergency was originally declared on 3 March 2026 and, on 11 June 2026, had been extended until September 2026. The restricted areas include major state institutions, such as Parliament/Red House, Woodford Square, the Office of the Prime Minister, the Office of the Director of Public Prosecutions, President’s House and the Police Administration Building. LATT questioned whether such wide exclusion zones are rationally connected and proportionate to the stated security objectives of the State of Emergency. It called on the authorities to review the order, publish clear geographic guidance on its application, and explain the legal basis and necessity for each designated zone. LATT also raised concern that arrests linked to protest activity outside the apparent geographic scope of the order could undermine public confidence and create uncertainty about what conduct is prohibited.
The intervention followed the arrest of activist Alyssa Phillip and her mother, Camille Caresquero, during Labour Day activities in Fyzabad. CAFRA Trinidad and Tobago, a feminist civil-society organisation, separately condemned the arrests as a troubling development for freedom of expression and assembly, warning that action against Phillip could intimidate others advocating for police transparency, accountability and access to justice. Together, these developments indicate that the restrictions imposed under the State of Emergency and their enforcement are affecting a widening range of civil-society actors and may deter public advocacy.

Title: President Samia labels some activism a security threat, sparking debate over civic rights
Content:
Tanzanian President Samia Suluhu Hassan has issued a stern warning to people who identify as activists, accusing them of engaging in terrorism actions. She said such actions, including disrupting peace and destroying property and infrastructure, are intended to intimidate the public and undermine the country's development, stressing that the government will not tolerate them. President Samia made the remarks on Thursday, 9 July 2026, at the State House in Zanzibar during the signing of the Joint Political Reconciliation Declaration between the ruling Chama Cha Mapinduzi (CCM) and ACT-Wazalendo.
Her remarks came about a week after Prime Minister Mwigulu Nchemba said he had no respect for activists while speaking during a visit to Mara Region on 1 July 2026. The Prime Minister accused some activists of acting against the country's interests and exploiting unrest for personal gain. He also claimed they had consistently attacked national leaders, including the fourth- and fifth-phase presidents, regardless of their contributions to the country.
On 9 July 2026, while swearing in 655 newly admitted advocates at Judicial Square, Tanzania's Chief Justice, George Masaju, urged lawyers to remain professional and avoid becoming activists, stressing that they should perform their duties in line with the laws governing the legal profession. Earlier, on 31 May 2026, Government Chief Spokesperson Gerson Msigwa accused some self-described activists and their foreign sponsors of encouraging Tanzanian youth to spread insults and division instead of contributing to the country's development. The strongest public rebuttal came from Bishop Benson Bagonza of the Evangelical Lutheran Church in Tanzania (ELCT), Karagwe Diocese. Speaking on 9 July he questioned whether Tanzania's founding leaders, Julius Nyerere and Abeid Karume, were themselves activists, arguing that it was contradictory to demonize activism when the nation was built by people who fought for social and political change. Lawyer and activist Jebra Kambole also defended activism, saying activists raise issues of public concern and that digital platforms have expanded citizens' ability to participate in public debate and hold leaders accountable.
These contrasting views reflect a widening debate in Tanzania, with the government portraying some forms of activism as a threat to national stability, while critics argue that activism is a legitimate tool for accountability and democratic participation.

Title: Institutional tension surrounding the change of government in Colombia
Content:
The transition process between President Gustavo Petro’s government and President-elect Abelardo de la Espriella’s transition team is at its most critical stage following the suspension of the transition talks, a decision taken after an exchange of accusations between the two teams. The national government announced the suspension of technical meetings, stating that there were insufficient guarantees of institutional respect to continue the process, after spokespeople close to the president-elect made  public allegations regarding alleged acts of corruption and suggested that the transition process should be turned into a political audit of the outgoing government.
For his part, the president-elect backed the suspension, arguing that current conditions do not allow for a transparent process to take place, and reiterated that his team would continue to gather information through other institutional channels. At the same time, the Comptroller General’s Office convened a technical working group with the aim of facilitating the continued exchange of information and reducing the risk of disruption to the handover of administrative responsibilities scheduled for 7 August.
The standoff has been accompanied by statements from President Petro questioning the electoral process and by a response from the president-elect, who has denounced attempts to delegitimise his victory. Although both sides have publicly stated that they will respect the constitutional mandate and the date of the handover of power, disagreements persist over how the handover should take place and the scope of each team’s responsibilities. The situation has prompted calls from various institutional sectors, including the Ombudsman’s Office , to preserve democratic stability and ensure an orderly transition that prioritises the public interest over political confrontation.

Title: Public solidarity for journalist amid pressure on critical voices
Content:
In May 2026, Mohamad Barakat published a public solidarity post on Facebook and X with journalist and political analyst Ibrahim Reihan, warning that critical and opposition voices are being kept under fear and intimidation. Barakat framed the pattern as an effort by a political party to maintain dissenting voices in a permanent state of fear while keeping journalists occupied defending themselves. Lebanon Debate reported on 13 May 2026 that Reihan stated his remarks had been deliberately extracted from context, and that he had filed six complaints before the Court of Cassation Public Prosecutor against persons whom he accused of incitement to kill, criminal defamation, damage to the standing of the state and judiciary, and moral forgery. Reihan also argued that media-related expression should fall under the jurisdiction of the Publications Court rather than general criminal prosecution.
This event is not only a dispute among political commentators. It reflects a wider pressure cycle in which public speech on sensitive security and political issues can trigger online accusation, legal escalation, counter-litigation  and reputational attacks. It can have a deterrent effect on journalists, researchers, activists, and civil society actors who comment on armed actors, state authority, security policy, or conflict-related developments. Further online amplification, legal steps or security-related complaints could deepen the negative effect on freedom of expression and digital safety.

Title: Mandatory one year re-registration period for CSOs commences as the Associations Act comes into effect
Content:
On 1 July 2026, Papua New Guinea's new Associations Incorporation Act 2023 came into effect, replacing the long-standing 1966 legislation governing incorporated associations. The new law introduces a mandatory one year re-registration period for all existing incorporated associations, requiring organisations to update their governance documents, committee information, and compliance records with the Investment Promotion Authority (IPA) by 30 June 2027. Associations that fail to re-register within the prescribed timeframe risk being deregistered or incurring late compliance penalties.









For civil society organisations (CSOs), the reforms are expected to strengthen governance, transparency and accountability in alignment with anti-money laundering and counter terrorist financing (AML/CTF) standards. However, this transition may also likely create short-term administrative and financial pressures, particularly for smaller organisations with limited capacity to meet the new compliance obligations. Development partners and donors may require evidence of successful re-registration as part of funding and due diligence processes. As the transition period progresses, CSOs are expected to prioritise compliance to ensure continued legal recognition and access to funding opportunities.

Title: Malaysia’s newly passed Cybercrimes Bill 2026
Content:
On 1 July 2026, the Cybercrimes Bill 2026 was passed in the Malaysian Parliament to replace the outdated Computer Crimes Act 1997. While meant to address modern cyber offences like AI scams and identity theft, a report by ARTICLE 19 warns that its vague language and broad scope risk turning the bill into a weapon for state censorship. Coming at a time when digital freedoms in Malaysia are already under fire, the bill effectively hands the government a new tool to suppress dissent, compounding existing overreach under the Communication and Multimedia Act 1998 (CMA), the Cybersecurity Act, and the Online Safety Act (ONSA).
Key concerns of the bill include surveillance and censorship abuses, significant unchecked enforcement powers as well as deficient safeguards. The bill’s primary danger lies in its lack of human rights and procedural safeguards, granting the state unaccountable control over computer-related activities. Warrantless searches and seizures are allowed if “an authorised officer is satisfied" that "he has reasonable cause to believe" that obtaining a search warrant would "adversely affect" the investigation. These authorised officers include any police officer, public officer, or officer of the Commission (Malaysian Communication and Multimedia Commission (MCMC)) as determined by the Minister.
Under the provisions of Section 36, authorised officers can compel the disclosure of passwords, encryption or decryption codes, and hardware or software. Furthermore, Sections 38 and 39 allow them to order the preservation and forced disclosure of user data simply if they deem it “reasonably required” for an investigation. Permitting such invasive access in the absence of independent judicial oversight directly violates the right to privacy and invites systemic surveillance abuse.

Title: Journalist Mourad Atmimou remanded in custody over social media posts
Content:
On 7 July 2026, the Algerian journalist and blogger Mourad Atmimou was arrested by plainclothes officers whilst he was in the Kessi cafeteria, opposite the Hasnaoua university campus in Tizi Ouzou. After two days in police custody, he was brought before the public prosecutor and then before the investigating judge at the Azazga court, who ordered, on 9 July 2026, his remand in custody. He is being prosecuted for several offences, including glorifying terrorism, insulting state symbols and spreading hate speech, in connection with posts shared on social media, some of which related to the parliamentary elections of 2 July 2026.
This case comes against a backdrop of a growing number of prosecutions against journalists, bloggers and content creators for their public statements. Organisations defending human rights and press freedom have condemned the use of particularly serious criminal charges against online publications, arguing that this practice contributes to further restricting freedom of expression and press freedom in Algeria.

Title: Rights groups urge FIFA to revoke World Cup 2026 broadcast rights for junta-linked telecom Mytel amidst erasure of democratic symbols
Content:
In June 2026, the advocacy group Justice for Myanmar (JfM) forcefully condemned FIFA's decision to grant exclusive 2026 World Cup broadcasting rights to Mytel, a telecommunications firm deeply embedded with the Myanmar military regime. Mytel operates as a joint venture between the military-controlled Myanmar Economic Corporation (MEC) and Viettel, an enterprise controlled by the Vietnamese military. Because MEC is subjected to strict sanctions from the US, UK, EU, Canada, and Australia for bankrolling the junta's atrocity crimes, rights groups argue that FIFA’s deal blatantly violates international human rights due diligence standards. Activists warn that revenue generated from subscription fees and advertising on Mytel's streaming platforms will directly subsidize the military's capacity to purchase munitions and suppress dissent.
Concurrently, the military regime has escalated its systematic campaign to erase the country's democratic memory. Throughout June 2026, the junta executed coordinated operations to forcibly remove National League for Democracy (NLD) signboards and symbols from party offices and public spaces across the country. Party officials described this physical erasure as a clear indication that the junta continues to view the ousted, democratically elected ruling party as a significant political threat, attempting to obliterate its lasting influence on public consciousness.

Title: Candidates elected in the general election have been detained as part of investigations into electoral fraud
Content:
A few days after the parliamentary elections on 2 July 2026, several legal proceedings were brought against elected candidates in various wilayas on suspicion of electoral fraud. In Oran, the investigating judge at the Oued Tlélat court ordered the remand in custody of an elected candidate from the Sawt Echaab (Voice of the People) party, as well as several election officials, as part of an investigation into alleged irregularities during the vote. In Djelfa, a separate investigation led to the remand in custody of eight people, whilst two female candidates, one of whom was elected, were placed under judicial supervision. According to published reports, an arrest warrant had also been issued for another elected candidate.
These cases, which were opened immediately after the results were announced, raise questions about the integrity of the electoral process and the mechanisms for vetting candidates and monitoring voting procedures. They come at a time when several political figures had already expressed concerns regarding the transparency of the election and are likely to undermine public confidence in representative institutions.

Title: State agents raid the premises of Casa de la Mujer in Santa Cruz de la Sierra
Content:
On 19 June 2026, more than 20 Bolivian state officials, including members of the Bolivian Police, personnel from the General Directorate of Migration, and officials from the Ministry of Government, entered the premises of the feminist organization Casa de la Mujer in Santa Cruz de la Sierra. According to available information, the operation was carried out without the presentation of a judicial warrant or any explanation of its legal basis.
During the operation, officials entered spaces used for psychological and legal support and forced women survivors of violence who were receiving assistance to interrupt their sessions, identify themselves, and be photographed and filmed. Casa de la Mujer reported that these actions violated the inviolability of the home (Art. 25.I of the Political Constitution of the State), the right to dignity and personal liberty (Art. 22 of the Political Constitution of the State), and the prohibition of revictimization established in Articles 33 and 35 of Law No. 348, in addition to constituting an act of harassment against human rights defenders.
The incident generated a broad response from civil society. The UNITAS network, which brings together 24 civil society organizations, issued an institutional statement, while more than 60 social and human rights organizations signed a joint communiqué expressing concern about the intervention. The Ombudsperson’s Office later reported that it opened a case ex officio to follow up on the events.
This case occurs in a context of high sociopolitical conflict and growing concerns regarding the State’s treatment of civil society organizations. The intervention in a space that provides care and shelter to women in vulnerable situations contributes to generating an intimidating effect among feminist and human rights organizations by reinforcing the perception of risk of potential state interventions without a clear public explanation of their legal basis. In addition to the direct impact on those receiving services and the interruption of support, the operation weakens guarantees for the safe exercise of freedom of association and the defense of human rights. The lack of clarification of the events and of measures to prevent recurrence could set a negative precedent for the enabling environment, the functioning of civil society organizations, and the protection of fundamental rights in Bolivia.

Title: State Police Bill addresses long-running problems with centralized policing but requires stronger safeguards
Content:
On 24 June 2026, the Nigerian Senate approved the State Police Bill, which advances with safeguards for decentralised policing in Nigeria. The bill had already passed the House of Representative on 10 June 2026 and proposes a constitutional framework for establishing State Police Services alongside a restructured Federal Police Service. It aims to improve local response to insecurity while adding national minimum standards, oversight commissions, and limits on political abuse. The Bill thus seeks to amend the 1999 Constitution so each State may establish its own police service, while the Federal Police retains responsibility for federal policing, the Federal Capital Territory, federal assets, interstate and national-security matters. To take effect, the Bill still requires approval of the State Houses of Assembly and the President’s assent.
The bill could shift policing from a highly centralised model to a constitutional federal–state framework, improving responsiveness, accountability, and protection of rights. If fully adopted and implemented, it would alter Nigeria’s security architecture, redistribute policing powers, and set new national standards for how police powers are exercised across the federation. This is particularly significant considering long-running problems with police concentration and abuse risks. The current model has been widely criticised for weak local responsiveness and for enabling arbitrary use of police power. The bill tries to address that by expressly banning partisan, ethnic, religious, or personal misuse of police authority, protecting tenure, and requiring oversight by police service commissions and the National Police Council.
However, for the bill to effectively improve policing, it needs to incorporate stronger accountability safeguards as the assessment conducted by a coalition of 30 civil society organisations found. Security governance experts, policy analysts, and governance advocates have similarly published detailed assessments discussing strengths of the proposed dual-police model, risks of political capture, funding sustainability, accountability institutions, human rights protections. The possibility of creating new abuse risks if state-level oversight is politicised or underfunded makes civil society monitoring especially important at the ratification and implementation stages, because the real test will be whether safeguards are enforceable in practice rather than only on paper.

Title: National Identity Management Commission Act aims to improve responsive governance but raises risks to fundamental freedoms
Content:
On 26 June 2026, President Tinubu signed The National Identity Management Commission (NIMC) Act 2026, modernising Nigeria’s identity system and boosting security. The new law harmonises previously fragmented identity databases, mandates interoperability between NIMC and agencies such as immigration, and strengthens the integrity and use of the National Identification Number (NIN). Officials said these changes will improve public service delivery, speed up digital transformation, deepen the digital economy, and enhance national security by making identity verification more reliable and automated.
By requiring agencies to integrate with the national identity system and enabling NIMC to act as a Root Certification Authority for PKI, the Act can make government services more responsive and easier to access through verified digital credentials, while also creating formal channels for identity-based service delivery and inclusion measures for vulnerable groups. The law also embeds stronger data‑protection measures, criminalises unauthorised access and identity abuse with stiffer penalties, and establishes technical trust layers (PKI, multipurpose card) that improve authentication and reduce fraud risk, thereby improving the security of digital transactions and personal data when properly implemented.
However, centralising identity and expanding mandatory NIN use for many public and private services raises specific risks to fundamental freedoms. While the Act includes safeguards, it also creates risks of surveillance, exclusion, and privacy erosion. In terms of inclusion of marginalized communities, mandatory linkage of NIN to services can restrict access for those who cannot obtain or prove NIN. Additionally, expanded data sharing increases the chance of intrusive profiling or state monitoring, and heavy criminalisation of certain identity‑related acts could be used to chill legitimate civic activity if due‑process and oversight are weak. The long-term impact of the law will therefore depend on implementation, oversight, and whether safeguards against misuse, exclusion, and rights violations are effectively enforced.

Title: New legal uncertainties arise after Mazariegos’ inauguration as rector of the University of San Carlos
Content:
Even after his controversial inauguration on 1 July 2026, Walter Mazariegos’ continued tenure as rector of the University of San Carlos of Guatemala (USAC) raises new questions of legal uncertainty. During the first session of the University Superior Council (CSU) an institutional legal opinion was disclosed that holds that the Temporary Certificate of No Pending Claims (finiquito), issued by the Office of the Comptroller General of Accounts (CGC), does not constitute a mandatory requirement to serve as rector.
USAC’s argument is grounded in the principle of legal specificity, asserting that the university’s Organic Law should prevail over the Law on Probity and Responsibilities of Public Officials and Employees. However, legal experts have publicly questioned this interpretation, noting that standards of probity, transparency, and accountability apply to authorities responsible for managing public resources, including autonomous institutions.
This new element deepens the existing controversy surrounding Mazariegos’ re-election, previously challenged by students, faculty, university professionals, Indigenous authorities, and civil society organizations due to allegations of a lack of transparency and irregularities in the university electoral process. The current debate continues to raise concerns about the consistent application of institutional oversight mechanisms and the ability of public authorities to ensure accountability.
The case is relevant to the enabling environment for civil society given USAC’s role as the country’s only public university and its participation in second-degree electoral processes and institutional spaces that influence the composition of key state bodies. The consolidation of an interpretation that limits probity mechanisms could weaken transparency standards and set a negative precedent for accountability and the rule of law in Guatemala.
La controversia mantiene vigentes los cuestionamientos sobre la permanencia de Mazariegos en el cargo y amplía el debate sobre la aplicación de los mecanismos de probidad, transparencia y rendición de cuentas en la USAC. Asimismo, adquiere especial importancia por la participación de la USAC en procesos de elección de segundo grado y en espacios institucionales que inciden en la conformación de órganos clave del Estado.

Title: BudgIT’s budget analysis brings transparency into public finance and facilitates public debate
Content:
On 15 June 2026, civic organization BudgIT published its 2026 Federal Government Approved Budget Analysis, which reviews Nigeria’s approved budget, fiscal assumptions, debt burden, and sectoral allocations. It highlights a total budget of N68.32 trillion against projected revenue of N36.87 trillion, leaving a large financing gap covered by borrowing, and notes that debt service alone will take N15.81 trillion.
The analysis also emphasizes major concerns around revenue realism, tax reforms, inflation, and debt sustainability, while pointing to spending priorities such as security, infrastructure, agriculture, health, and education. It also notes weak social-sector allocations.
The analysis contributes to budget transparency with the identified concerns picked up by other CSO, thereby shaping public debate around the 2026 budget. With civil society commentary and media responses echoing the same budget-related concerns, the report is feeding into wider accountability conversations, pushing for better disclosure and strong scrutiny of public spending. Over time, it can contribute to systemic change by improving budget credibility and public accountability.

Title: Constitutional Amendment No. 3 and its implications for democratic governance and institutional independence
Content:
On 7 July 2026, the President of Zimbabwe H.E. Emmerson Mnangagwa, signed Constitutional Amendment No. 3 (CAB3) into law in Zimbabwe. The amendments, described as wide-ranging, include provisions that extend the electoral term of the President, Parliament, and local authorities from five to seven years, thereby extending the current electoral cycle to 2030 and postponing the next harmonised elections initially expected in 2028. The amendments also change the manner in which the President is elected, removing direct election by citizens and transferring this responsibility to Parliament. These changes represent a significant constitutional shift with far-reaching political and institutional implications.
The new constitutional arrangements further allow the President to appoint an additional 10 senators, increasing the chamber’s size to 90 from 80. They also relocate aspects of the voter registration process from the Zimbabwe Electoral Commission (ZEC) to the Registrar General, while a commission is expected to determine delimitation. In the same context, the amendment also reports the scrapping of public interviews for the judiciary. Taken together, these measures indicate that the implications of the amendment extend beyond the electoral timeline, affecting governance, representation, administrative processes, and judicial appointment procedures.
Critics of CAB3 argued that, given the nature and effect of the proposed amendments, the changes should have been subjected to a referendum in accordance with Zimbabwe’s constitutional framework. They maintained that altering the duration of elected terms and the electoral system without a direct public vote undermined constitutional safeguards and the principle of popular sovereignty. The decision not to pursue a referendum therefore became a major point of legal and political contestation, raising questions among opponents regarding the legitimacy and acceptance of any constitutional order extending beyond the electoral cycle originally set to end in 2028.

Title: Nigerian court orders payment in SLAPP case against SERAP
Content:
On 5 May 2026, the Federal Capital Territory High Court ordered the Socio-Economic Rights and Accountability Project (SERAP) to pay ₦100 million in damages to two Department of State Services (DSS) officials for defamation, alongside ₦1 million in litigation costs, public apologies, and 10% annual post-judgment interest. The ruling stems from allegations made by SERAP in September 2024 that DSS operatives unlawfully entered its Abuja office after the organisation called for investigations into alleged corruption at the Nigerian National Petroleum Company Limited (NNPCL) and fuel price increases.
The case, initially filed as a ₦5.5 billion claim, was described by SERAP as a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP). Following the judgment, SERAP rejected the ruling as “totally unacceptable”, filed an appeal on 8 May 2026 with Senior Advocates of Nigeria, and applied for a stay of execution, arguing that the case represents an attempt to restrict civic accountability and free expression. The DSS maintained that its visit was routine and that its officers were subjected to false allegations.
Civil society organisations and human rights groups have warned that the ruling could have a chilling effect on freedom of expression, particularly for journalists, activists, and accountability organisations such as SERAP. They argue that the judgment risks expanding the use of defamation law as a tool to intimidate civil society and restrict public-interest advocacy, reinforcing concerns that the case reflects characteristics of a Strategic Lawsuit Against Public Participation (SLAPP). The dispute is also notable as a rare defamation suit brought by security operatives against a civil society organisation in Nigeria, raising broader concerns about the use of litigation in contexts involving state accountability and oversight.
The case remains ongoing, with SERAP’s appeal pending as of June 2026, and observers note that its outcome could set an important precedent for the legal framework governing civic space and government accountability in Nigeria, particularly in balancing defamation claims with the protection of public-interest speech. The developments point to growing tensions between state security institutions and civil society organisations in Nigeria, with potential implications for the enabling environment for civic advocacy, oversight, and public-interest litigation, as well as the protection of fundamental freedoms.

Title: Sentencing of Judge Anas Hammadi to one year’s imprisonment on appeal to be served immediately
Content:
On 2 July 2026, the Criminal Division of the Tunis Court of Appeal upheld the sentence of one year’s imprisonment handed down to Judge Anas Hammadi, President of the Tunisian Magistrates’ Association, for “obstructing the freedom to work”, whilst ordering the immediate enforcement of the sentence. The proceedings relate to the role he played in organising the magistrates’ strike in June 2022, which was triggered by the dismissal of 57 magistrates by presidential decree.
This decision has raised serious concerns amongst national and international organisations defending human rights and the independence of the judiciary, which see it as a further step in the pressure being exerted against magistrates critical of the judicial reforms undertaken since 2022. Several observers believe that this conviction could have a deterrent effect on judges’ freedom of association, freedom of assembly, their freedom of expression and their ability to defend the independence of the judiciary. The case forms part of a broader context in which the guarantees of judicial independence are being called into question and civic space in Tunisia is increasingly restricted.

Title: Legislative proposal No. 1.659/2024 risks restricting international funding and the activities of civil society organizations
Content:
Bill No. 1,659/2024, currently under consideration by the Chamber of Deputies’ Committee on Foreign Affairs and National Defense (CREDN), has received a new substitute text submitted by its rapporteur, Deputy Evair Vieira de Melo (Republicanos-ES), which significantly alters the scope of the original proposal. While the initial bill sought to regulate the receipt of foreign funding by civil society organizations (CSOs), the substitute that was introduced on July 3, 2026, adopts a more restrictive approach by imposing limitations on international funding for these organizations and linking such support to potential risks to national sovereignty. In addition, the substitute includes restrictions on the participation of internationally funded organizations in public policy-making bodies, limitations on certain partnerships with public authorities, and obstacles to advocacy and strategic litigation activities.
The proposal is still awaiting deliberation by the committee. If approved, it will proceed through the subsequent stages of the legislative process in the Chamber of Deputies, including consideration by the other competent committees before a possible vote by the Chamber's plenary. Should the bill ultimately be approved in the form of the substitute text currently under consideration, it would represent a significant shift in the regulatory framework governing civil society organizations in Brazil..
It constitutes a serious threat to CSOs’ access to resources with international funding an essential source of financial support for organizations working in areas such as human rights, environmental protection, civic participation, institutional strengthening, social assistance, public health, education and public policy oversight. Additionally, the proposed restrictions could also affect organizations that redistribute funding to local initiatives, thereby reducing financial support available to community-based organizations, grassroots movements and local groups that frequently depend on intermediary mechanisms for international cooperation.
Beyond its financial implications, the substitute introduces restrictions that may affect the participation of civil society organizations in public policy councils, advisory committees and other institutional decision-making spaces, as well as certain forms of advocacy and strategic litigation. If implemented, these measures could alter the relationship between the State and civil society by reducing opportunities for the institutional participation of organizations receiving international funding.
From a systemic perspective, the proposal represents a potential shift in Brazil’s regulatory framework for civil society by moving away from a transparency-based approach towards a model centred on restricting organizations according to the origin of their funding. The very introduction and institutional consideration of legislation that frames international funding for civil society organizations as a potential threat to national sovereignty already constitutes an indicator of a narrowing civic space. Even if its legal effects ultimately do not materialize, the proposal reflects a shift in institutional discourse and in the way civil society organizations and international cooperation are framed, with the potential to generate chilling effects on civic participation and the financial sustainability of the sector.
The current stage of the legislative process therefore warrants continued monitoring as a potential risk to Brazil’s enabling environment for civil society.

Title: Sedition Case of Five Human Rights Defenders regarding the Seminar on Right to Self-Determination and Conducting Mock-Referendum
Content:
Witness examination hearings are underway in a sedition case against five Malayu human rights defenders and activists—Mr. Irfan Umar, Mr. Hakim Pongtigor, Mr. Artef Sohko, Mr. Hussen Bue-nae, and Mr. Sareef Salaeman. The charges stem from their organization of and/or participation in a public seminar held on 7 June 2023 concerning the right to self-determination of the Patani people in southern Thailand.
The Court has scheduled prosecution witness hearings for 7–10 and 14–17 July 2026, while defence witness hearings are set for 18–20 August 2026. If convicted, the five defenders face prison sentences of up to seven years.
The prosecution of these five human rights defenders represents a significant deterioration of the enabling environment for civil society in Thailand. The use of sedition charges against individuals for organizing and participating in a peaceful seminar on self-determination raises serious concerns regarding the criminalization of legitimate human rights activities and the suppression of public debate on politically sensitive issues.

Title: Jamaica signs Memorandum of Understanding with the USA regarding the transit of third country nationals
Content:
On 18 June 2026, the Government of Jamaica publicly announced that it had entered into a Memorandum of Understanding (MOU) with the United States of America to facilitate the temporary transit of Third Country Nationals (TCNs) through Jamaica. According to the Deputy Prime Minister and Minister of National Security and Peace, Dr. Horace Chang, the agreement permits up to 25 individuals every two weeks to transit through Jamaica while arrangements are made for onward travel to a third country or their country of origin.
The Government stated that the agreement received Cabinet approval and was negotiated by several government ministries and the Attorney General's Chambers. Operational guidelines governing implementation, including screening procedures, oversight mechanisms, suspension provisions, accommodation arrangements, and security checks, remain under development. Government officials also indicated that Jamaica retains discretion to refuse individuals proposed for transfer and that persons seeking to remain in Jamaica would be required to apply for asylum through the courts.
The announcement raises broader governance and human rights considerations concerning transparency, public access to information, oversight, and the implementation of international agreements affecting asylum seekers and migrants. While the Government has provided some information regarding the agreement, aspects of its operational framework and human rights safeguards remain to be fully articulated.

Title: Activist Mohamed Saïd Riahi sentenced to eighteen months’ imprisonment without parole
Content:
The court in Aïn Témouchent sentenced Mohamed Saïd Riahi to eighteen months’ imprisonment without parole and a fine of 200,000 dinars. Title: Legislator Threatens Journalist Over Publication of an Investigation Into His Assets
Content:
On 30 June 2026, the freedom of expression advocacy organization Fundamedios made public information regarding threats that journalist Gonzalo Piña allegedly received from individuals close to National Assembly member Jorge Guevara, a member of the governing party's legislative bloc. According to Piña's testimony, the threats began after he published an investigation into an insolvency proceeding that the legislator was reportedly facing.
On 24 June, the journalist received an anonymous phone call in which he was threatened with physical violence for carrying out his work. The following day, Assembly member Guevara himself contacted him via message, describing the report as an attack and claiming that the judicial proceeding had already been dismissed. Piña stated that his investigation was based on publicly available information and that the electronic system of the Judicial Branch contained no record indicating that the case had been closed.
Two months earlier, another journalist reported a similarly aggressive attitude by the same assembly member on social media, suggesting a possible pattern of obstruction of freedom of expression and press freedom, particularly against journalists who scrutinize the work of the National Assembly.
Fundamedios and the Fundación Ciudadanía y Desarrollo publicly condemned these incidents and urged the competent authorities to investigate the source of the threats, while also calling on elected officials to respect journalistic work and public oversight.

Title: Harassment of members of youth organisations during government-organised consultation forum
Content:
On 2 July 2026, during a government-organised Accountability Summit at the ‘Manthabiseng Convention Centre in Maseru, members of youth organisations reported that police officers and members of the Lesotho Defence Force (LDF) harassed young participants who were peacefully expressing their views through placards. According to a joint statement issued by the organisations on 3 July 2026, security personnel questioned participants, confronted them and confiscated their placards despite there being no allegations of violence or disruption of the proceedings.
The Accountability Summit was held between 1 and 3 July 2026 and was established to enable citizens and civil society organisations to engage directly with national leaders, ask questions, seek clarification and provide feedback on governance and service delivery issues. It was presented as a platform to strengthen accountability, transparency and public participation.
Following the incident, the youth organisations called for public apologies from the Lesotho Mounted Police Service and the LDF, assurances that peaceful expression would be protected at future public events, condemnation of the conduct by the summit organisers and implementation of measures to safeguard civic participation.
While the summit itself reflected an increase state openness to civil society engagement, the harassment experienced by the youth organisations interfered with their constitutional right to freedom of expression and undermined the purpose of the summit as a forum for open public participation. Compared to other instances of protester intimidation, the intimidation of peaceful participants during the summit carries particular weight as it occurred during a forum specifically established to promote dialogue and citizen participation.
The broader impact of this event remains to be seen and will depend on the response of state authorities and the summit organizers. If not addressed properly, the incident is expected to discourage citizens and civil society organisations from participating openly in future public consultations and accountability processes. This would weaken confidence in government-led participation mechanisms and reduce the effectiveness of forums designed to strengthen transparency and accountability. Conversely, a prompt response by the responsible authorities, including acknowledging the incident, safeguarding participants’ rights and ensuring that future public engagement processes remain free from intimidation, could reinforce public trust and strengthen the enabling environment for civic participation.

Title: Detention of members of a civil society/ Rastafarian group during demonstration outside King’s House

Title: Two independent bookstores abruptly barred from Hong Kong Book Fair
Content:

Title: Closure of 74-year-old HKU student publication “Undergrad” (學苑)
Content:
On 28 June 2026, Undergrad (學苑), the historic student publication of the University of Hong Kong (HKU), announced it would cease operations after 74 years. The official editorial board stated it was unable to form a new leadership team for the 2026 term despite multiple recruitment drives, forcing the publication to close. In a farewell statement, the board declared that the publication's "historical role in society has come to an end."
Founded in 1952, Undergrad had been a key student organisation that pushed the boundaries of intellectual thought. It tested critical ideas and highly sensitive political ideas, most notably in 2014 when it published an influential book and articles exploring the concepts of Hong Kong nationalism and self-determination. This intellectual defiance later drew direct, severe condemnation from the city's Chief Executive.
The publication's closure reflects the wider systemic collapse of student organisations in Hong Kong. The general atmosphere, including a pervasive chilling effect, has left students unwilling to take up leadership roles in campus journalism and civic bodies.

Title: National security arrest of independent bookstore founder Wong Man-huen
Content:

Authorities accused her of displaying and selling publications with seditious intent under the city's national security laws, as well as money laundering. Leticia Wong was released on 26 June 2026 on police bail.
Prior to the arrest, the bookstore had displayed political song lyrics in its window and sold symbolic candles for the 37th anniversary of the Tiananmen crackdown on 4 June 2026. Following the police raid and the arrest of its founders, Hunter Bookstore has remained closed.

Title: Military personnel allegedly torture civilians in Moyamba District, Southern Sierra Leone
Content:
On 27 June 2026, two men working as casual laborers were allegedly tortured by military personnel in Senehun Town, Kamajei Chiefdom in Moyamba District, after being accused of stealing fertilizers from their employer. According to a video circulating on social media, they were subjected to inhuman and degrading treatment by military personnel who were forcing them to confess to the crime.  The men were allegedly beaten, chained to a metal frame, and forced to confess, with uniformed men seen striking them with sticks and other objects as they cried out in pain. The Republic of Sierra Leone Armed Forces (RSLAF) have been quick to condemn the act and affirmed to investigate the incident, with the two men referred for medical treatment.
Right groups and Civil Society Organizations have condemned the actions of the military personnel with considerations for the rule of law, and human rights of both men. The Human Rights Defenders Network Sierra Leone (HRDN-SL) and the Campaign for Human Rights and Development International (CHRDI) are calling for an impartial and independent investigation, and urged authorities to pursue criminal and disciplinary action against any personnel found responsible, while providing appropriate compensation and support to the victims including both medical and psychological support. CHRDI is further calling for the immediate suspension of the implicated personnel pending full investigation. Both organizations believe the action of RSLAF restore public trust for the institution in the face of such violations.

Title: Widespread civil society opposition forces government to put deliberations of Transparency bill on hold
Content:
Following the widespread rejection of a Draft Law on Transparency and Publicity of the Management of Interests by civil society organizations, professional association, and business chambers, the Constitutional Affairs and General Legislation commission of the Chamber of Deputies decided on 16 June 2026 to postpone advancing the law and revert it for further negotiations. The Commissions were forced to make this decision when none of the 26 convened speakers supported its official text, thereby publicly recognizing the need for modifications.
The Draft Law had been submitted by the Executive Branch to Congress for expedited treatment on 26 May 2026 and proposes a Public Registry of Interest Managers with prior registration obligations, quarterly reports and criminal sanctions for non-compliance. Civil society organizations criticized the broad definition of “interest management” applicable not only to corporate lobbying but also to civil society advocacy as well as the equation of legal persons incorporated abroad with foreign influence, thereby instilling suspicion against organizations working with international cooperation.
More than 190 civil society organizations raised alerts regarding the expected impact of the draft law on the enabling environment. Pablo Secchi of Poder Ciudadano summarized that the draft law “is not regulating corporate lobbying, this is criminalizing citizen participation." In its presentations to the commission, Red Encuentro also highlighted the structural exclusion resulting from the draft: "access is consolidated for the actors with greater institutional power and the participation of those with fewer resources is hindered or prevented." Amnesty International Argentina, the ACIJ and Fundación Huésped issued similar public alerts.
Apart from civil society actors, the draft was also rejected by the business sector including the United States Chamber of Commerce in Argentina and the Argentine Industrial Union with CSO actors suspecting that their opposition may have contributed significantly to the ruling party's decision to postpone further processing of the draft law.
While the postponement is an important victory for civil society, the commission will continue to meet to develop the law. Given that the ruling party does not have enough votes to quickly push through its version of the law, this creates an important opportunity for opposition actors and civil society to develop an alternative text that regulates corporate lobbying while protecting civil society participation. Instead of regulating advocacy through punitive means, civil society continues to call for strengthened participation mechanisms through formal and permanent spaces for public consultation.
Beyond the legislative process itself, the experience of civil society’s collective articulation rejecting the law and achieving a joint public positioning across sectoral and ideological divisions constitute valuable organizational capital to sustain advocacy in the next stages and respond to future threats of the enabling environment. In terms of civic culture, the debate publicly established the distinction between making the lobby of economic interests transparent and criminalizing citizen participation.
